Let fame, that all hunt after in their lives, / Live registered upon our brazen tombs, / And then grace us in the disgrace of death; / When, spite of cormorant devouring time, / Th' endeavour of this present breath may buy / That honour which shall bate his scythe's keen edge, / And make us heirs of all eternity. / Therefore, brave conquerors, for so you are / That war against your own affections / And the huge army of the world's desires, / Our late edict shall strongly stand in force. / Navarre shall be the wonder of the world; / Our court shall be a little academe, / Still and contemplative in living art. / You three, Berowne, Dumaine and Longaville, / Have sworn for three years' term to live with me, / My fellow-scholars, and to keep those statutes / That are recorded in this schedule here. / Your oaths are passed, and now subscribe your names, / That his own hand may strike his honour down / That violates the smallest branch herein. / If you are armed to do as sworn to do, / Subscribe to your deep oaths, and keep it too.

Let the fame that everyone chases in life be carved on our brass tombs, and honour us even when death has disgraced us. In spite of greedy, devouring time, what we achieve while we are alive can buy the kind of honour that blunts time's sharp scythe and makes us heirs to eternity. So, brave conquerors (and you are conquerors, since you are at war with your own feelings and the huge army of worldly desires), our recent decree will stand firm. Navarre will be the wonder of the world; our court will be a little academy, quiet and thoughtful, devoted to the art of living. You three, Berowne, Dumaine and Longaville, have sworn to live with me for three years as fellow students, and to keep the rules written down in this document. You have taken the oath; now sign your names, so that anyone who breaks the smallest rule strikes down his own honour with his own hand. If you are ready to do what you swore, sign your solemn oaths, and keep them too.
I am resolved. 'Tis but a three years' fast. / The mind shall banquet, though the body pine. / Fat paunches have lean pates, and dainty bits / Make rich the ribs, but bankrupt quite the wits.
I've made up my mind. It's only a three-year fast. The mind will feast, though the body starves. Fat bellies have thin brains, and rich food fattens the ribs but bankrupts the wits.

My loving lord, Dumaine is mortified. / The grosser manner of these world's delights / He throws upon the gross world's baser slaves. / To love, to wealth, to pomp, I pine and die, / With all these living in philosophy.
My dear lord, Dumaine has given up the flesh. He hands the cruder pleasures of this world to the world's lower slaves. I die to love, wealth and show, and find them all in philosophy instead.

I can but say their protestation over. / So much, dear liege, I have already sworn, / That is, to live and study here three years. / But there are other strict observances: / As not to see a woman in that term, / Which I hope well is not enrolled there; / And one day in a week to touch no food, / And but one meal on every day beside, / The which I hope is not enrolled there; / And then to sleep but three hours in the night, / And not be seen to wink of all the day, / When I was wont to think no harm all night, / And make a dark night too of half the day, / Which I hope well is not enrolled there. / O, these are barren tasks, too hard to keep, / Not to see ladies, study, fast, not sleep.

I can only repeat what they've promised. I've already sworn this much, my lord: to live and study here for three years. But there are other strict rules too: not to see a woman for that time, which I very much hope isn't written down there; to eat nothing one day a week, and only one meal on every other day, which I hope isn't written down there either; and to sleep only three hours a night and never be seen to nod off during the day, when I used to sleep soundly all night and turn half the day into night as well. I hope that isn't written down there. Oh, these are empty tasks, too hard to keep: no ladies, study, fasting, no sleep.
Your oath is passed to pass away from these.
You swore an oath to give up those things.
Let me say no, my liege, an if you please. / I only swore to study with your Grace / And stay here in your court for three years' space.
Let me say no to that, my lord, if you don't mind. I only swore to study with Your Grace and stay at your court for three years.
You swore to that, Berowne, and to the rest.
You swore to that, Berowne, and to all the rest.
By yea and nay, sir, then I swore in jest. / What is the end of study, let me know?
Then, by yes and no, sir, I swore as a joke. What is the purpose of study? Tell me.
Why, that to know which else we should not know.
Why, to know what we otherwise wouldn't know.
Things hid and barred, you mean, from common sense?
You mean things hidden and closed off from ordinary understanding?
Ay, that is study's god-like recompense.
Yes, that is the god-like reward of study.

Come on, then, I will swear to study so, / To know the thing I am forbid to know: / As thus, to study where I well may dine, / When I to feast expressly am forbid; / Or study where to meet some mistress fine, / When mistresses from common sense are hid; / Or, having sworn too hard-a-keeping oath, / Study to break it, and not break my troth. / If study's gain be thus, and this be so, / Study knows that which yet it doth not know. / Swear me to this, and I will ne'er say no.

All right then, I'll swear to study in that way, to know what I am forbidden to know. For example: to study where I can find a good dinner when I'm strictly forbidden to feast; or where to meet a lovely mistress when mistresses are hidden from ordinary view; or, having sworn an oath too hard to keep, to study how to break it without breaking my word. If that's what study gains, then study teaches what it doesn't yet know. Swear me to that and I'll never say no.
These be the stops that hinder study quite, / And train our intellects to vain delight.
Those are exactly the obstacles that block real study and train our minds to idle pleasure.

Why, all delights are vain, but that most vain / Which, with pain purchased, doth inherit pain: / As painfully to pore upon a book / To seek the light of truth, while truth the while / Doth falsely blind the eyesight of his look. / Light seeking light doth light of light beguile; / So, ere you find where light in darkness lies, / Your light grows dark by losing of your eyes. / Study me how to please the eye indeed / By fixing it upon a fairer eye, / Who dazzling so, that eye shall be his heed, / And give him light that it was blinded by. / Study is like the heaven's glorious sun, / That will not be deep-searched with saucy looks; / Small have continual plodders ever won, / Save base authority from others' books. / These earthly godfathers of heaven's lights, / That give a name to every fixed star, / Have no more profit of their shining nights / Than those that walk and wot not what they are. / Too much to know is to know naught but fame, / And every godfather can give a name.

Why, all pleasures are empty, but the emptiest is the one bought with pain that only earns more pain: like painfully poring over a book to find the light of truth, while all that time the truth is blinding your eyes. Eyes looking for light rob themselves of light; so before you find where light lies hidden in the darkness, your own light goes dark because you've lost your eyesight. Teach me instead how to please the eye by fixing it on a lovelier eye, a woman's: even if that dazzles it, that eye will be its guide and give back the light it was blinded by. Study is like the glorious sun in the sky, which won't let impudent eyes search it deeply. Constant plodders have never gained much except second-hand authority from other people's books. Astronomers, those earthly godfathers who name every fixed star, get no more good from their starry nights than people who walk about not knowing what the stars are. Knowing too much just means knowing names, and any godfather can give a name.
How well he's read, to reason against reading.
How learned he is, at arguing against learning!
Proceeded well, to stop all good proceeding.
He argues well, to stop all good progress.
He weeds the corn, and still lets grow the weeding.
He weeds out the corn and lets the weeds keep growing.
The spring is near when green geese are a-breeding.
Spring is coming, when baby geese are hatching.
What does that have to do with anything?
Fit in his place and time.
It fits its place and its time.
Berowne is like an envious sneaping frost / That bites the first-born infants of the spring.
Berowne is like a spiteful, nipping frost that kills the first-born buds of spring.

Well, say I am. Why should proud summer boast / Before the birds have any cause to sing? / Why should I joy in any abortive birth? / At Christmas I no more desire a rose / Than wish a snow in May's new-fangled shows, / But like of each thing that in season grows. / So you, to study now it is too late, / Climb o'er the house to unlock the little gate.

Suppose I am. Why should proud summer show off before the birds have any reason to sing? Why should I be glad of something born too early? At Christmas I don't want a rose any more than I want snow in May's fresh blossoms; I like each thing that grows in its own season. You're starting to study too late, like climbing over the roof to unlock the little garden gate.
Well, sit you out. Go home, Berowne. Adieu.
Well, stay out of it, then. Go home, Berowne. Goodbye.

No, my good lord, I have sworn to stay with you, / And though I have for barbarism spoke more / Than for that angel knowledge you can say, / Yet confident I'll keep what I have sworn / And bide the penance of each three years' day. / Give me the paper, let me read the same, / And to the strictest decrees I'll write my name.

No, my good lord, I've sworn to stay with you. And though I've spoken more for ignorance than you can say for that angel, knowledge, I'm still confident I'll keep my oath and suffer the penance of every day of the three years. Give me the paper; let me read it, and I'll sign my name to the strictest rules.
How well this yielding rescues thee from shame.
How well your giving in saves you from disgrace.
[Reads] Item, That no woman shall come within a mile of my court. / Hath this been proclaimed?
[Reads] 'Item: no woman shall come within a mile of my court.' Has this been announced?
Let's see the penalty. [Reads] On pain of losing her tongue. Who / devised this penalty?
Let's see the penalty. [Reads] 'On pain of losing her tongue.' Who thought up this penalty?
To fright them hence with that dread penalty.
To scare them away with that terrible punishment.

A dangerous law against gentility. / [Reads] Item, If any man be seen to talk with a woman within the / term of three years, he shall endure such public shame as the rest of / the court can possibly devise. / This article, my liege, yourself must break, / For well you know here comes in embassy / The French King's daughter, with yourself to speak— / A mild of grace and complete majesty— / About surrender up of Aquitaine / To her decrepit, sick, and bedrid father. / Therefore this article is made in vain, / Or vainly comes th' admired Princess hither.

A law dangerous to good manners. [Reads] 'Item: if any man is seen talking with a woman during the three years, he shall suffer whatever public shame the rest of the court can think up.' You'll have to break this rule yourself, my lord, because you know very well that the French King's daughter is coming here as an ambassador to speak with you, a lady of gentle grace and perfect majesty, about handing over Aquitaine to her old, sick, bedridden father. So either this rule is pointless, or the admired Princess is coming here for nothing.
What say you, lords? Why, this was quite forgot.
What do you say, lords? Why, we completely forgot about this.

So study evermore is overshot. / While it doth study to have what it would, / It doth forget to do the thing it should; / And when it hath the thing it hunteth most, / 'Tis won as towns with fire: so won, so lost.

That's how study always overshoots its target. While it studies to get what it wants, it forgets to do what it ought to do; and when it gets the thing it was hunting most, it's like a town won by burning it: won and lost at the same moment.
We must of force dispense with this decree. / She must lie here on mere necessity.
We'll have to set this rule aside. She has to stay here; we have no choice.

Necessity will make us all forsworn / Three thousand times within this three years' space; / For every man with his affects is born, / Not by might mastered, but by special grace. / If I break faith, this word shall speak for me: / I am forsworn on mere necessity. / So to the laws at large I write my name, / And he that breaks them in the least degree / Stands in attainder of eternal shame. / Suggestions are to other as to me; / But I believe, although I seem so loath, / I am the last that will last keep his oath.

Necessity will make us all break our oaths three thousand times in these three years. Every man is born with his passions, and they can't be mastered by force, only by God's special grace. If I break my word, this will be my defence: I broke my oath because I had to. So I sign my name to all the laws, and whoever breaks the smallest of them is condemned to eternal shame. Temptations come to others as they come to me; but I believe, though I seem so unwilling, I will be the last to keep his oath to the last.
But is there no quick recreation granted?
But is there no lively entertainment allowed?

Ay, that there is. Our court, you know, is haunted / With a refined traveller of Spain, / A man in all the world's new fashion planted, / That hath a mint of phrases in his brain; / One who the music of his own vain tongue / Doth ravish like enchanting harmony, / A man of complements, whom right and wrong / Have chose as umpire of their mutiny. / This child of fancy, that Armado hight, / For interim to our studies shall relate / In high-born words the worth of many a knight / From tawny Spain lost in the world's debate. / How you delight, my lords, I know not, I, / But I protest I love to hear him lie, / And I will use him for my minstrelsy.

Yes, there is. Our court, as you know, is haunted by an elegant traveller from Spain, a man dressed in all the world's newest fashions, who has a whole mint of phrases in his head; a man who is enchanted by the music of his own vain voice as if it were magic harmony; a man of such fine manners that right and wrong would choose him as referee in their quarrel. This creature of fantasy, called Armado, will entertain us between our studies by telling us, in high-flown words, about the worth of many knights from sunburnt Spain who were lost in the world's wars. I don't know what you enjoy, my lords, but I confess I love to hear him lie, and I'll use him as my entertainer.
Armado is a most illustrious wight, / A man of fire-new words, fashion's own knight.
Armado is a most famous fellow, a man of brand-new words, fashion's own knight.
Costard the swain and he shall be our sport, / And so to study three years is but short.
He and Costard the country lad will be our fun, and so three years of study will feel short.
Which is the Duke's own person?
Which one is the Duke himself?
This one, fellow. What do you want?
I myself reprehend his own person, for I am his Grace's farborough. But / I would see his own person in flesh and blood.
I myself represent his person, for I am His Grace's constable. But I would like to see his own person in flesh and blood.
Signior Arm… Arm… commends you. There's villainy abroad. This letter / will tell you more.
Signior Arm... Arm... sends his regards. There's villainy about. This letter will tell you more.
Sir, the contempts thereof are as touching me.
Sir, the contents of it concern me.
A letter from the magnificent Armado.
A letter from the magnificent Armado.
How long soever the matter, I hope in God for high words.
However trivial the matter, I hope to God for high-flown words.
A high hope for a low heaven. God grant us patience!
That's a lofty hope for a lowly kind of heaven. God give us patience!
Patience to listen, or to stop ourselves laughing?
To hear meekly, sir, and to laugh moderately, or to forbear both.
To listen meekly, sir, and laugh in moderation, or to do neither.
Well, sir, be it as the style shall give us cause to climb in the / merriness.
Well, sir, let's see whether the style gives us cause to climb up to laughter.
The matter is to me, sir, as concerning Jaquenetta. The manner of it / is, I was taken with the manner.
The matter concerns me, sir, and Jaquenetta. The way of it is, I was caught in the act.

In manner and form following, sir, all those three. I was seen with her / in the manor-house, sitting with her upon the form, and taken following / her into the park, which, put together, is "in manner and form / following". Now, sir, for the manner. It is the manner of a man to / speak to a woman. For the form—in some form.

In the manner and form following, sir, all three of them. I was seen with her in the manor house, sitting with her on a bench, and caught following her into the park. Put together, that's 'in manner and form following'. Now, sir, as for the manner: it's the manner of a man to speak to a woman. As for the form: in some form or other.
As it shall follow in my correction, and God defend the right!
That will follow in my punishment; and God defend the right!
Will you hear this letter with attention?
Will you listen carefully to this letter?
As we would hear an oracle.
As we would listen to an oracle.
Such is the simplicity of man to hearken after the flesh.
That's how simple man is, listening to the flesh.
[Reads] Great deputy, the welkin's vicegerent and sole dominator of / Navarre, my soul's earth's god and body's fostering patron—
[Reads] 'Great deputy, the sky's representative and sole ruler of Navarre, my soul's god on earth and my body's nourishing patron...'
Not a word of Costard yet.
Not a word about Costard yet.
It may be so; but if he say it is so, he is, in telling true, but so.
It may be so; but if he says it is so, he is, to tell the truth, only so-so.
Be to me, and every man that dares not fight.
Be quiet yourself, and so should every man who daren't fight.
Of other men's secrets, I beseech you.
About other men's secrets, I beg you.

[Reads] So it is, besieged with sable-coloured melancholy, I did / commend the black-oppressing humour to the most wholesome physic of thy / health-giving air; and, as I am a gentleman, betook myself to walk. The / time when? About the sixth hour, when beasts most graze, birds best / peck, and men sit down to that nourishment which is called supper. So / much for the time when. Now for the ground which? Which, I mean, I / walked upon. It is ycleped thy park. Then for the place, where? Where, / I mean, I did encounter that obscene and most preposterous event that / draweth from my snow-white pen the ebon-coloured ink, which here thou / viewest, beholdest, surveyest, or seest. But to the place where? It / standeth north-north-east and by east from the west corner of thy / curious-knotted garden. There did I see that low-spirited swain, that / base minnow of thy mirth—

[Reads] 'So it is: besieged by black melancholy, I entrusted my dark, oppressive mood to the healthy medicine of your health-giving air, and, as I am a gentleman, went for a walk. The time when? About the sixth hour, when animals graze most, birds peck best and men sit down to the nourishment called supper. So much for the time when. Now for the ground which: which, I mean, I walked on. It is called your park. Then for the place where: where, I mean, I came upon that obscene and most unnatural event that draws the ebony ink from my snow-white pen, which you now view, behold, survey or see. But as for the place where: it lies north-north-east and by east from the west corner of your intricately laid-out garden. There I saw that low-spirited peasant, that lowly little fish of your amusement...'
[Reads] Which, as I remember, hight Costard—
[Reads] 'who, as I recall, is called Costard...'
[Reads] Sorted and consorted, contrary to thy established / proclaimed edict and continent canon, which with, O, with—but with this / I passion to say wherewith—
[Reads] 'keep company and consort, against your announced decree and law of chastity, with... oh, with... but it pains me to say with what...'

[Reads] With a child of our grandmother Eve, a female; or, for thy / more sweet understanding, a woman. Him, I, as my ever-esteemed duty / pricks me on, have sent to thee, to receive the meed of punishment, by / thy sweet Grace's officer, Antony Dull, a man of good repute, carriage, / bearing, and estimation.

[Reads] 'with a child of our grandmother Eve, a female, or, for your sweeter understanding, a woman. As my ever-honoured duty urges me, I have sent him to you to receive his due punishment, in the charge of Your Grace's officer, Antony Dull, a man of good reputation, conduct, bearing and standing.'
Me, an't shall please you; I am Antony Dull.
That's me, if you please; I am Antony Dull.

[Reads] For Jaquenetta, so is the weaker vessel called which I / apprehended with the aforesaid swain, I keep her as a vessel of thy / law's fury, and shall, at the least of thy sweet notice, bring her to / trial. Thine, in all compliments of devoted and heartburning heat of / duty, / Don Adriano de Armado.

[Reads] 'As for Jaquenetta (that is what the weaker vessel is called whom I caught with the aforesaid peasant), I am keeping her as a vessel for your law's fury, and will bring her to trial at your least command. Yours, in all the courtesies of devoted and heart-burning heat of duty, Don Adriano de Armado.'
This is not so well as I looked for, but the best that ever I heard.
That's not as good as I hoped, but it's the best I ever heard.
Ay, the best for the worst. But, sirrah, what say you to this?
Yes, the best of the worst. But, fellow, what do you say to this?
Sir, I confess to the girl.
I do confess much of the hearing it, but little of the marking of it.
I confess I heard a lot of it, but paid little attention to it.
It was proclaimed a year's imprisonment to be taken with a wench.
It announced a year in prison for anyone caught with a wench.
I was taken with none, sir. I was taken with a damsel.
I wasn't caught with a wench, sir. I was caught with a damsel.
This was no damsel neither, sir; she was a virgin.
She wasn't a damsel either, sir; she was a virgin.
It is so varied too, for it was proclaimed "virgin".
If it were, I deny her virginity. I was taken with a maid.
If it did, I deny she's a virgin. I was caught with a maid.
This maid will not serve your turn, sir.
This maid will serve my turn, sir.
This maid will help me fine, sir.
Sir, I will pronounce your sentence: you shall fast a week with bran / and water.
Sir, I'll pronounce your sentence: you will fast for a week on bran and water.
I had rather pray a month with mutton and porridge.
I'd rather pray for a month on mutton and soup.
And Don Armado shall be your keeper. / My Lord Berowne, see him delivered o'er; / And go we, lords, to put in practice that / Which each to other hath so strongly sworn.
And Don Armado will be your jailer. My Lord Berowne, see that he's handed over. And let's go, lords, and put into practice what we've each sworn to the others so firmly.
I'll lay my head to any good man's hat / These oaths and laws will prove an idle scorn. / Sirrah, come on.
I'll bet my head against any good man's hat that these oaths and laws will turn out to be an empty joke. Come on, fellow.

I suffer for the truth, sir; for true it is I was taken with / Jaquenetta, and Jaquenetta is a true girl. And therefore welcome the / sour cup of prosperity! Affliction may one day smile again, and till / then, sit thee down, sorrow.

I suffer for the truth, sir; for it's true I was caught with Jaquenetta, and Jaquenetta is a true girl. So welcome, sour cup of prosperity! Affliction may smile on me again one day; and till then, sit down, sorrow.
Boy, what sign is it when a man of great spirit grows melancholy?
Boy, what does it mean when a man of great spirit grows melancholy?
A great sign, sir, that he will look sad.
It's a great sign, sir, that he'll look sad.
Why, sadness is one and the selfsame thing, dear imp.
Why, sadness and melancholy are one and the same thing, dear imp.
No, no, O Lord, sir, no.
No, no, oh Lord, sir, no.
How canst thou part sadness and melancholy, my tender juvenal?
How can you separate sadness from melancholy, my tender youth?
By a familiar demonstration of the working, my tough signior.
By a simple demonstration of how they work, my tough sir.
Why tough signior? Why tough signior?
Why tender juvenal? Why tender juvenal?
I spoke it, tender juvenal, as a congruent epitheton appertaining to / thy young days, which we may nominate tender.
I said it, tender youth, as a fitting description belonging to your young days, which we may call tender.
And I, tough signior, as an appertinent title to your old time, which / we may name tough.
And I said it, tough sir, as a suitable title for your old age, which we may call tough.
How mean you, sir? I pretty and my saying apt, or I apt, and my saying / pretty?
What do you mean, sir? That I'm pretty and my saying is apt, or that I'm apt and my saying is pretty?
Little pretty, because little. Wherefore apt?
A little bit pretty, because little. And why apt?
Speak you this in my praise, master?
Do you mean this as praise, master?
I will praise an eel with the same praise.
I could praise an eel the same way.
What, that an eel is ingenious?
What, that an eel is clever?
I do say thou art quick in answers. Thou heat'st my blood.
I'm saying you're quick with answers. You're making me angry.
I love not to be crossed.
I don't like to be crossed.
[Aside] He speaks the mere contrary; crosses love not him.
[Aside] He's got it backwards: crosses don't like him. (Crosses were coins stamped with a cross; he's broke.)
I have promised to study three years with the Duke.
I've promised to study for three years with the Duke.
You may do it in an hour, sir.
You could do it in an hour, sir.
How many is one thrice told?
How much is one three times over?
I am ill at reckoning. It fitteth the spirit of a tapster.
I'm bad at arithmetic. It suits the mind of a barman.
You are a gentleman and a gamester, sir.
You're a gentleman and a gambler, sir.
I confess both. They are both the varnish of a complete man.
I admit to both. They are both the polish of a complete man.
Then I am sure you know how much the gross sum of deuce-ace amounts to.
Then I'm sure you know how much a two and a one on the dice add up to.
It doth amount to one more than two.
They come to one more than two.
Which the base vulgar do call three.
Which the common people call three.

Why, sir, is this such a piece of study? Now here's three studied ere / ye'll thrice wink. And how easy it is to put "years" to the word / "three", and study three years in two words, the dancing horse will / tell you.

Well, sir, is that such a hard piece of study? There, you've studied 'three' before you can blink three times. And how easy it is to add 'years' to 'three', and study three years in two words, the performing horse could tell you.
A very fine figure of speech!

I will hereupon confess I am in love; and as it is base for a soldier / to love, so am I in love with a base wench. If drawing my sword against / the humour of affection would deliver me from the reprobate thought of / it, I would take desire prisoner, and ransom him to any French courtier / for a new-devised curtsy. I think scorn to sigh; methinks I should / outswear Cupid. Comfort me, boy. What great men have been in love?

I'll confess, then, that I am in love; and since it is low for a soldier to love, I am in love with a low-born girl. If drawing my sword against the passion of love would free me from the sinful thought of it, I would take desire prisoner and sell him to any French courtier in exchange for a newly invented bow. I scorn to sigh; I think I could out-swear Cupid himself. Comfort me, boy. Which great men have been in love?
Most sweet Hercules! More authority, dear boy, name more; and, sweet my / child, let them be men of good repute and carriage.
Most sweet Hercules! More examples, dear boy, name more; and, my sweet child, let them be men of good reputation and carriage.
Samson, master. He was a man of good carriage, great carriage, for he / carried the town gates on his back like a porter, and he was in love.
Samson, master. He was a man of good carriage, great carriage, because he carried the town gates on his back like a porter; and he was in love.
O well-knit Samson, strong-jointed Samson! I do excel thee in my rapier / as much as thou didst me in carrying gates. I am in love too. Who was / Samson's love, my dear Moth?
O well-built Samson, strong-limbed Samson! I beat you with my rapier as much as you beat me at carrying gates. I'm in love too. Who was Samson's love, my dear Moth?
Of all the four, or the three, or the two, or one of the four.
All four of them, or three, or two, or one of the four.
Tell me precisely of what complexion.
Tell me exactly what her complexion was.
Is that one of the four complexions?
Is that one of the four complexions?
As I have read, sir; and the best of them too.
So I've read, sir; and the best of them, too.
Green indeed is the colour of lovers. But to have a love of that / colour, methinks Samson had small reason for it. He surely affected her / for her wit.
Green is certainly the colour of lovers. But I think Samson had little reason to love a woman that colour. Surely he loved her for her wit.
It was so, sir, for she had a green wit.
He did, sir, because she had a green wit.
My love is most immaculate white and red.
My love is the most spotless white and red.
Most maculate thoughts, master, are masked under such colours.
The most spotted thoughts, master, hide behind those colours.
My father's wit and my mother's tongue assist me!
May my father's wit and my mother's tongue help me!
Sweet invocation of a child, most pretty, and pathetical!
A child's sweet prayer, very pretty and moving!

If she be made of white and red, / Her faults will ne'er be known; / For blushing cheeks by faults are bred, / And fears by pale white shown. / Then if she fear, or be to blame, / By this you shall not know, / For still her cheeks possess the same / Which native she doth owe. / A dangerous rhyme, master, against the reason of white and red.

If she is made of white and red, you'll never know her faults; because faults make cheeks blush red, and fear makes them pale white. So if she is afraid or guilty, you won't be able to tell from this, because her cheeks always keep the colours she was born with. A dangerous rhyme, master, against the case for white and red.
Is there not a ballad, boy, of the King and the Beggar?
Isn't there a ballad, boy, about the King and the Beggar girl?
The world was very guilty of such a ballad some three ages since, but I / think now 'tis not to be found; or if it were, it would neither serve / for the writing nor the tune.
The world was guilty of a ballad like that about three generations ago, but I don't think it can be found now; or if it could, it would be no good for either the words or the tune.

I will have that subject newly writ o'er, that I may example my / digression by some mighty precedent. Boy, I do love that country girl / that I took in the park with the rational hind Costard. She deserves / well.
I'll have that subject written again, so that I can excuse my lapse with a great example. Boy, I love that country girl I caught in the park with that reasoning animal Costard. She deserves well.
[Aside] To be whipped: and yet a better love than my master.
[Aside] She deserves to be whipped; and yet she's a better lover than my master deserves.
Sing, boy. My spirit grows heavy in love.
Sing, boy. My spirit grows heavy with love.
And that's great marvel, loving a light wench.
And that's a great wonder, loving a light woman.
Forbear till this company be past.
Wait until these people have gone past.

Sir, the Duke's pleasure is that you keep Costard safe; and you must / suffer him to take no delight, nor no penance, but he must fast three / days a week. For this damsel, I must keep her at the park. She is / allowed for the dey-woman. Fare you well.

Sir, the Duke wants you to keep Costard securely; and you mustn't let him have any pleasure, nor any penance either, except that he must fast three days a week. As for this damsel, I have to keep her at the park. She's employed as the dairymaid. Goodbye.
I do betray myself with blushing.—Maid.
My blushes are giving me away. Maid.
I will visit thee at the lodge.
I will visit you at the lodge.
I know where it is situate.
Villain, thou shalt fast for thy offences ere thou be pardoned.
Villain, you will fast for your crimes before you are pardoned.
Well, sir, I hope when I do it I shall do it on a full stomach.
Well, sir, I hope when I fast I'll do it on a full stomach.
I am more bound to you than your fellows, for they are but lightly / rewarded.
Then I owe you more than your servants do, because they're only lightly rewarded.
Take away this villain. Shut him up.
Take this villain away. Lock him up.
Come on, you lawbreaking slave, away with you!
Let me not be pent up, sir. I will fast being loose.
Don't let me be shut up, sir. I'll fast while I'm loose.
No, sir, that were fast and loose. Thou shalt to prison.
No, sir, that would be 'fast and loose' (a cheat's trick). You're going to prison.
Well, if ever I do see the merry days of desolation that I have seen, / some shall see.
Well, if I ever see the merry days of misery I've seen before, some people will see.

Nay, nothing, Master Moth, but what they look upon. It is not for / prisoners to be too silent in their words, and therefore I will say / nothing. I thank God I have as little patience as another man, and / therefore I can be quiet.

Nothing, Master Moth, except what they look at. It's not right for prisoners to be too silent in their words, so I'll say nothing. Thank God I have as little patience as the next man, so I can keep quiet.

I do affect the very ground, which is base, where her shoe, which is / baser, guided by her foot, which is basest, doth tread. I shall be / forsworn, which is a great argument of falsehood, if I love. And how / can that be true love which is falsely attempted? Love is a familiar; / Love is a devil. There is no evil angel but Love. Yet was Samson so / tempted, and he had an excellent strength; yet was Solomon so seduced, / and he had a very good wit. Cupid's butt-shaft is too hard for / Hercules' club, and therefore too much odds for a Spaniard's rapier. / The first and second cause will not serve my turn; the passado he / respects not, the duello he regards not. His disgrace is to be called / boy, but his glory is to subdue men. Adieu, valour; rust, rapier; be / still, drum, for your manager is in love. Yea, he loveth. Assist me, / some extemporal god of rhyme, for I am sure I shall turn sonnet. / Devise, wit; write, pen; for I am for whole volumes in folio.

I love the very ground, which is lowly, where her shoe, which is lowlier, guided by her foot, which is lowliest, steps. If I love, I'll break my oath, which is strong evidence of falseness. And how can a love be true that is begun falsely? Love is an evil spirit; Love is a devil. There is no bad angel except Love. Yet Samson was tempted like this, and he was extremely strong; Solomon was seduced like this, and he was very wise. Cupid's blunt arrow is too hard for Hercules' club, so it is far too much for a Spaniard's rapier. The rules of duelling won't help me: Cupid doesn't care for the forward thrust or the formal duel. It shames him to be called a boy, but his glory is to conquer men. Farewell, courage; rust, rapier; be quiet, drum, for your master is in love. Yes, he loves. Help me, some god of improvised rhyme, for I'm sure I'll turn into a sonnet. Invent, wit; write, pen; for I'm good for whole volumes in folio.

Now, madam, summon up your dearest spirits. / Consider who the King your father sends, / To whom he sends, and what's his embassy. / Yourself, held precious in the world's esteem, / To parley with the sole inheritor / Of all perfections that a man may owe, / Matchless Navarre; the plea of no less weight / Than Aquitaine, a dowry for a queen. / Be now as prodigal of all dear grace / As Nature was in making graces dear / When she did starve the general world beside / And prodigally gave them all to you.

Now, madam, gather your finest powers. Think who the King your father is sending, to whom he is sending her, and what her mission is: you yourself, prized by the whole world, to negotiate with the sole heir of every perfection a man can have, the matchless King of Navarre; and the matter is nothing less than Aquitaine, a dowry fit for a queen. So be as lavish now with all your precious charm as Nature was when she made such charms precious by starving the rest of the world and giving them all to you.

Good Lord Boyet, my beauty, though but mean, / Needs not the painted flourish of your praise. / Beauty is bought by judgement of the eye, / Not uttered by base sale of chapmen's tongues. / I am less proud to hear you tell my worth / Than you much willing to be counted wise / In spending your wit in the praise of mine. / But now to task the tasker: good Boyet, / You are not ignorant, all-telling fame / Doth noise abroad Navarre hath made a vow, / Till painful study shall outwear three years, / No woman may approach his silent court. / Therefore to's seemeth it a needful course, / Before we enter his forbidden gates, / To know his pleasure; and in that behalf, / Bold of your worthiness, we single you / As our best-moving fair solicitor. / Tell him the daughter of the King of France, / On serious business craving quick dispatch, / Importunes personal conference with his Grace. / Haste, signify so much, while we attend, / Like humble-visaged suitors, his high will.

Good Lord Boyet, my beauty, ordinary as it is, doesn't need the painted decoration of your praise. Beauty is judged by the eye that sees it, not sold off by the cheap patter of pedlars. I'm less proud to hear you tell my worth than you are eager to be thought clever for spending your wit on praising mine. But now to set the task-setter a task. Good Boyet, you know that rumour, which tells everything, is spreading the news that Navarre has made a vow: no woman may come near his silent court until three years of painful study are over. So it seems necessary to us, before we go through his forbidden gates, to find out what he wants; and for that, trusting your worth, we choose you as our most persuasive advocate. Tell him the daughter of the King of France, on serious business that needs a quick settlement, asks to speak with His Grace in person. Hurry and tell him, while we wait for his royal answer like humble petitioners.
Proud of employment, willingly I go.
Proud to be employed, I go willingly.
All pride is willing pride, and yours is so.
All pride is willing pride, and yours is that kind.
Who are the votaries, my loving lords, / That are vow-fellows with this virtuous Duke?
Who are the men who have taken the vow, my dear lords, along with this virtuous Duke?

I know him, madam. At a marriage feast / Between Lord Perigort and the beauteous heir / Of Jaques Falconbridge, solemnized / In Normandy, saw I this Longaville. / A man of sovereign parts, he is esteemed, / Well fitted in arts, glorious in arms. / Nothing becomes him ill that he would well. / The only soil of his fair virtue's gloss, / If virtue's gloss will stain with any soil, / Is a sharp wit matched with too blunt a will, / Whose edge hath power to cut, whose will still wills / It should none spare that come within his power.

I know him, madam. I saw this Longaville in Normandy, at the wedding feast of Lord Perigort and the beautiful heiress of Jaques Falconbridge. He is thought a man of outstanding gifts, well trained in learning, glorious in battle. Anything he wants to do well suits him. The only stain on the shine of his fine qualities, if such a shine can be stained at all, is a sharp wit joined to a will too blunt: his wit has the power to cut, and his will always wants it to spare no one who comes within its reach.
Some merry mocking lord, belike. Is't so?
Some merry, mocking lord, I suppose. Is that right?
They say so most that most his humours know.
Those who know his moods best say so most.
Such short-lived wits do wither as they grow. / Who are the rest?
Wits like that, short-lived, wither as they grow. Who are the others?

The young Dumaine, a well-accomplished youth, / Of all that virtue love for virtue loved; / Most power to do most harm, least knowing ill, / For he hath wit to make an ill shape good, / And shape to win grace though he had no wit. / I saw him at the Duke Alençon's once; / And much too little of that good I saw / Is my report to his great worthiness.

The young Dumaine, a very accomplished young man, loved for his virtue by everyone who loves virtue. He has most power to do harm and knows least about evil, for he has the wit to make a bad shape look good, and the looks to win favour even if he had no wit. I saw him once at the Duke of Alençon's; and what I say about his great worth is much less than the good I saw.

Another of these students at that time / Was there with him, if I have heard a truth. / Berowne they call him, but a merrier man, / Within the limit of becoming mirth, / I never spent an hour's talk withal. / His eye begets occasion for his wit, / For every object that the one doth catch / The other turns to a mirth-moving jest, / Which his fair tongue, conceit's expositor, / Delivers in such apt and gracious words / That aged ears play truant at his tales, / And younger hearings are quite ravished, / So sweet and voluble is his discourse.

Another of these students was there with him at the time, if what I've heard is true. They call him Berowne; but I never spent an hour talking with a merrier man, within the limits of decent fun. His eye finds the chances for his wit: everything the eye catches, the wit turns into a laughing joke, which his fine tongue, the interpreter of his ideas, delivers in such fitting and graceful words that old men play truant from their business to hear his stories, and young listeners are completely carried away, his talk is so sweet and fluent.
God bless my ladies! Are they all in love, / That every one her own hath garnished / With such bedecking ornaments of praise?
God bless my ladies! Are they all in love, that each one has dressed up her own man with such decorations of praise?

Navarre had notice of your fair approach, / And he and his competitors in oath / Were all addressed to meet you, gentle lady, / Before I came. Marry, thus much I have learned: / He rather means to lodge you in the field, / Like one that comes here to besiege his court, / Than seek a dispensation for his oath, / To let you enter his unpeopled house.

Navarre had heard of your arrival, and he and his partners in the oath were all ready to meet you, gentle lady, before I got there. But this much I've learned: he means to lodge you out in the open, like someone who has come to besiege his court, rather than seek release from his oath to let you into his empty house.
Fair Princess, welcome to the court of Navarre.
Fair Princess, welcome to the court of Navarre.
"Fair" I give you back again, and "welcome" I have not yet. The roof of / this court is too high to be yours, and welcome to the wide fields too / base to be mine.
I give you back 'fair'; and as for 'welcome', I haven't had any yet. The roof of this court is too high to be yours, and a welcome in the open fields is too lowly to be mine.
You shall be welcome, madam, to my court.
You'll be welcome to my court, madam.
I will be welcome then. Conduct me thither.
Then I'll be welcome. Take me there.
Hear me, dear lady. I have sworn an oath.
Listen to me, dear lady. I have sworn an oath.
Our Lady help my lord! He'll be forsworn.
Our Lady help my lord! He's going to break it.
Not for the world, fair madam, by my will.
Not for the world, fair madam, if I can help it.
Why, will shall break it; will, and nothing else.
Why, desire will break it; desire, and nothing else.
Your ladyship is ignorant what it is.
Your ladyship doesn't know what the oath is.

Were my lord so, his ignorance were wise, / Where now his knowledge must prove ignorance. / I hear your Grace hath sworn out housekeeping. / 'Tis deadly sin to keep that oath, my lord, / And sin to break it. / But pardon me, I am too sudden bold. / To teach a teacher ill beseemeth me. / Vouchsafe to read the purpose of my coming, / And suddenly resolve me in my suit.

If my lord didn't know either, his ignorance would be wise, whereas now his knowledge turns out to be ignorance. I hear Your Grace has sworn to give up hospitality. It's a deadly sin to keep that oath, my lord, and a sin to break it. But forgive me, I'm too suddenly bold; it isn't right for me to teach a teacher. Please read the reason for my visit, and answer my request quickly.
Madam, I will, if suddenly I may.
Madam, I will, if I can do it quickly.
You will the sooner that I were away, / For you'll prove perjured if you make me stay.
You'll be the quicker to get me gone, because you'll break your oath if you make me stay.
[To Rosaline] Did not I dance with you in Brabant once?
[To Rosaline] Didn't I dance with you in Brabant once?
Did not I dance with you in Brabant once?
Didn't I dance with you in Brabant once?
How needless was it then / To ask the question!
Then how pointless it was to ask the question!
You must not be so quick.
'Tis long of you that spur me with such questions.
It's your fault, for spurring me on with such questions.
Your wit's too hot, it speeds too fast, 'twill tire.
Your wit is too hot; it gallops too fast; it will tire.
Not till it leave the rider in the mire.
Not before it throws its rider in the mud.
What time of day is it?
The hour that fools should ask.
The hour when fools ask questions.
Good luck to your mask, then.
Fair fall the face it covers.
And good luck to the face it covers.
And may it send you many lovers!
Amen, as long as you're not one of them.
Nay, then will I be gone.

Madam, your father here doth intimate / The payment of a hundred thousand crowns, / Being but the one half of an entire sum / Disbursed by my father in his wars. / But say that he or we, as neither have, / Received that sum, yet there remains unpaid / A hundred thousand more, in surety of the which / One part of Aquitaine is bound to us, / Although not valued to the money's worth. / If then the King your father will restore / But that one half which is unsatisfied, / We will give up our right in Aquitaine, / And hold fair friendship with his majesty. / But that, it seems, he little purposeth; / For here he doth demand to have repaid / A hundred thousand crowns, and not demands, / On payment of a hundred thousand crowns, / To have his title live in Aquitaine, / Which we much rather had depart withal, / And have the money by our father lent, / Than Aquitaine, so gelded as it is. / Dear Princess, were not his requests so far / From reason's yielding, your fair self should make / A yielding 'gainst some reason in my breast, / And go well satisfied to France again.

Madam, your father mentions here the payment of a hundred thousand crowns, which is only half of the whole sum my father spent on his wars. But suppose he or we had received that sum, though neither of us has: there would still be another hundred thousand unpaid, and as security for that, part of Aquitaine is pledged to us, although it isn't worth the money. So if the King your father will repay just that one unpaid half, we'll give up our right to Aquitaine and keep good friendship with His Majesty. But it seems that is not what he intends: here he demands to be repaid a hundred thousand crowns, rather than offering to pay a hundred thousand crowns to get his claim to Aquitaine back. We would much rather part with Aquitaine, stripped of value as it is, and have the money our father lent. Dear Princess, if his demands weren't so far from reasonable, your lovely self would make something in my heart give way against reason, and you'd go back to France well satisfied.
You do the King my father too much wrong, / And wrong the reputation of your name, / In so unseeming to confess receipt / Of that which hath so faithfully been paid.
You do my father the King a great wrong, and damage the good name of your own, by pretending not to have received what has been so faithfully paid.
I do protest I never heard of it; / And, if you prove it, I'll repay it back / Or yield up Aquitaine.
I swear I never heard of it; and if you prove it, I'll pay it back or give up Aquitaine.
We arrest your word. / Boyet, you can produce acquittances / For such a sum from special officers / Of Charles his father.
We hold you to your word. Boyet, you can produce receipts for that sum from the officials of his father, Charles.
So please your Grace, the packet is not come / Where that and other specialties are bound. / Tomorrow you shall have a sight of them.
If it please Your Grace, the package containing that and other documents hasn't arrived. Tomorrow you'll see them.

It shall suffice me; at which interview / All liberal reason I will yield unto. / Meantime receive such welcome at my hand / As honour, without breach of honour, may / Make tender of to thy true worthiness. / You may not come, fair Princess, in my gates, / But here without you shall be so received / As you shall deem yourself lodged in my heart, / Though so denied fair harbour in my house. / Your own good thoughts excuse me, and farewell. / Tomorrow shall we visit you again.

That will be good enough for me, and at that meeting I'll agree to any fair reasoning. In the meantime, accept such welcome from me as honour can offer to your true worth without breaking honour. You may not come inside my gates, fair Princess, but out here you'll be received so well that you'll feel you're lodged in my heart, though you're refused good lodging in my house. Your own kind thoughts will excuse me. Goodbye; we'll visit you again tomorrow.
Sweet health and fair desires consort your Grace.
Good health and happy wishes go with Your Grace.
Thy own wish wish I thee in every place.
I wish you the same everywhere you go.
Lady, I will commend you to mine own heart.
Lady, I'll commend you to my own heart.
Pray you, do my commendations; I would be glad to see it.
Please do give it my regards; I'd be glad to see it.
I would you heard it groan.
I wish you could hear it groan.
Will you prick't with your eye?
Will you pierce it with your eye?
Not at all; with my knife.
And keep you from living long.
I can't stay to thank you for that.
Sir, I pray you, a word. What lady is that same?
Sir, a word, please. Who is that lady?
The heir of Alençon, Katharine her name.
The heiress of Alençon; her name is Katharine.
A gallant lady. Monsieur, fare you well.
I beseech you a word. What is she in the white?
A word, please. Who is she in white?
A woman sometimes, an you saw her in the light.
A woman, sometimes, if you saw her in the light.
Perchance light in the light. I desire her name.
Perhaps light in the light (loose in her morals). I want her name.
She hath but one for herself; to desire that were a shame.
She has only one for herself; it would be shameful to want that.
Please, sir, whose daughter is she?
God bless your beard! (that is, curse your cheek!)
Good sir, be not offended. / She is an heir of Falconbridge.
Good sir, don't be offended. She is an heiress of the Falconbridges.
Nay, my choler is ended. / She is a most sweet lady.
Well, my anger is over. She is a very sweet lady.
Not unlike, sir; that may be.
Quite likely, sir; that may be.
What's her name in the cap?
What's the name of the one in the cap?
To her will, sir, or so.
To her own will, sir, more or less.
Farewell to me, sir, and welcome to you.
Goodbye to me, sir, and welcome to you (good riddance to you).
That last is Berowne, the merry madcap lord. / Not a word with him but a jest.
That last one is Berowne, the merry, madcap lord. Every word he says is a joke.
And every jest but a word.
And every joke is only a word.
It was well done of you to take him at his word.
You did well to take him up on his words.
I was as willing to grapple as he was to board.
I was as ready to grapple with him as he was to board me.
And wherefore not ships? / No sheep, sweet lamb, unless we feed on your lips.
And why not ships? We're not sheep, sweet lamb, unless we feed on your lips.
You sheep and I pasture. Shall that finish the jest?
You the sheep and I the pasture? Will that end the joke?
So you grant pasture for me.
As long as you give me grazing.
Not so, gentle beast. / My lips are no common, though several they be.
Not so, gentle beast. My lips are not common land, though they are two (and private).
To my future and to me.
Good wits will be jangling; but, gentles, agree. / This civil war of wits were much better used / On Navarre and his bookmen, for here 'tis abused.
Good wits will squabble; but, my friends, make peace. This civil war of wits would be much better used on Navarre and his bookworms; here it's wasted.
If my observation, which very seldom lies, / By the heart's still rhetoric disclosed with eyes, / Deceive me not now, Navarre is infected.
If my observation, which very rarely lies, isn't fooling me now about the silent language of the heart that shows through the eyes, Navarre is infected.
With that which we lovers entitle "affected".
With what we lovers call 'being in love'.

Why, all his behaviours did make their retire / To the court of his eye, peeping thorough desire. / His heart, like an agate, with your print impressed, / Proud with his form, in his eye pride expressed. / His tongue, all impatient to speak and not see, / Did stumble with haste in his eyesight to be; / All senses to that sense did make their repair, / To feel only looking on fairest of fair. / Methought all his senses were locked in his eye, / As jewels in crystal for some prince to buy; / Who, tend'ring their own worth from where they were glassed, / Did point you to buy them, along as you passed. / His face's own margent did quote such amazes / That all eyes saw his eyes enchanted with gazes. / I'll give you Aquitaine, and all that is his, / An you give him for my sake but one loving kiss.

Why, all his behaviour retreated into his eyes, peeping out with desire. His heart, like a seal-stone engraved with your picture, was proud of that image and showed its pride in his eyes. His tongue, impatient at being able to speak but not see, stumbled in its hurry to be in his eyes. All his senses ran to the sense of sight, just to feel themselves looking at the fairest of the fair. I thought all his senses were locked up in his eyes like jewels in a crystal case for a prince to buy, and from behind the glass they offered themselves and pointed you to buy them as you passed. His face was like the margin of a book, noting such wonder that every eye saw his eyes were bewitched by gazing. I'll give you Aquitaine and everything he owns if you'll give him just one loving kiss for my sake.
Come, to our pavilion. Boyet is disposed.
Come, to our tent. Boyet is in a joking mood.
But to speak that in words which his eye hath disclosed. / I only have made a mouth of his eye / By adding a tongue which I know will not lie.
I'm only putting into words what his eyes revealed. I've just made his eye into a mouth by adding a tongue that I know won't lie.
Thou art an old love-monger, and speakest skilfully.
You're an old love-dealer, and you talk cleverly.
He is Cupid's grandfather, and learns news of him.
He is Cupid's grandfather, and gets his news from him.
Then was Venus like her mother; for her father is but grim.
Then Venus took after her mother, because her father is very ugly.
Do you hear, my mad wenches?
Are you listening, my mad girls?
Ay, our way to be gone.
Yes: our way out of here.
You are too hard for me.
Warble, child, make passionate my sense of hearing.
Sing, child; fill my sense of hearing with passion.
Sweet air! Go, tenderness of years, take this key, give enlargement to / the swain, bring him festinately hither. I must employ him in a letter / to my love.
A sweet tune! Go, tender youth, take this key, set the peasant free and bring him here quickly. I need him to carry a letter to my love.
Master, will you win your love with a French brawl?
Master, are you going to win your love with a French brawl?
How meanest thou? Brawling in French?
What do you mean? Quarrelling in French?

No, my complete master; but to jig off a tune at the tongue's end, / canary to it with your feet, humour it with turning up your eyelids, / sigh a note and sing a note, sometime through the throat, as if you / swallowed love with singing love, sometime through the nose, as if you / snuffed up love by smelling love; with your hat penthouse-like o'er the / shop of your eyes, with your arms crossed on your thin-belly doublet / like a rabbit on a spit; or your hands in your pocket like a man after / the old painting; and keep not too long in one tune, but a snip and / away. These are compliments, these are humours; these betray nice / wenches that would be betrayed without these; and make them men of / note—do you note me?—that most are affected to these.

No, my perfect master; I mean dance a jig off the tip of your tongue, dance a canary to it with your feet, add to the mood by rolling up your eyes, sigh a note and sing a note, sometimes through your throat as if you were swallowing love by singing about love, sometimes through your nose as if you were sniffing up love by smelling it; with your hat pulled over your eyes like a shop awning, your arms folded over your thin waistcoat like a rabbit on a spit, or your hands in your pockets like a man in an old painting; and don't stay too long on one tune, just a snatch and away. These are the fashions, these are the tricks. They seduce fine girls who would be seduced anyway; and they make the men who go in for them men of note. Do you note me?
How hast thou purchased this experience?
How did you buy this experience?
With my penny's worth of observation.
'...the hobby-horse is forgotten.' (A line from a popular song.)
Are you calling my love a 'hobby-horse'?
No, master. The hobby-horse is but a colt, and your love perhaps a / hackney. But have you forgot your love?
No, master. The hobby-horse is only a colt, and your love is perhaps a hired hack. But have you forgotten your love?
Negligent student! Learn her by heart.
Careless student! Learn her by heart.
By heart and in heart, boy.
By heart and in heart, boy.
And out of heart, master. All those three I will prove.
And out of heart, master. I'll prove all three.

A man, if I live; and this, "by, in, and without," upon the instant: / "by" heart you love her, because your heart cannot come by her; "in" / heart you love her, because your heart is in love with her; and "out" / of heart you love her, being out of heart that you cannot enjoy her.

A man, if I live; and this 'by, in and out of' straight away. You love her 'by' heart, because your heart can't come by her; 'in' heart, because your heart is in love with her; and 'out of' heart, because you're disheartened that you can't have her.
And three times as much more, and yet nothing at all.
And three times as much again, and yet nothing at all.
Fetch hither the swain. He must carry me a letter.
Bring the peasant here. He must carry a letter for me.
A message well sympathized: a horse to be ambassador for an ass.
A well-matched errand: a horse to be ambassador for an ass.
Ha, ha, what are you saying?
Marry, sir, you must send the ass upon the horse, for he is very / slow-gaited. But I go.
Why, sir, you'll have to send the ass on the horse, because he's very slow on his feet. But I'm going.
The way is but short. Away!
It's only a short way. Go!
The meaning, pretty ingenious? / Is not lead a metal heavy, dull, and slow?
What do you mean, clever little one? Isn't lead a heavy, dull and slow metal?
Minime, honest master; or rather, master, no.
Not at all, honest master; or rather, master, no.
You are too swift, sir, to say so. / Is that lead slow which is fired from a gun?
You're too quick to say so, sir. Is lead slow when it's fired from a gun?
Sweet smoke of rhetoric! / He reputes me a cannon; and the bullet, that's he. / I shoot thee at the swain.
Sweet smoke of rhetoric! He takes me for a cannon, and he's the bullet. I fire you at the peasant.
A most acute juvenal, voluble and free of grace! / By thy favour, sweet welkin, I must sigh in thy face. / Most rude melancholy, valour gives thee place. / My herald is returned.
A very sharp youth, quick-tongued and full of charm! By your leave, sweet sky, I must sigh in your face. Most rude melancholy, courage gives way to you. My messenger has come back.
A wonder, master! Here's a costard broken in a shin.
A wonder, master! Here's a Costard (an apple-head) with a broken shin.
Some enigma, some riddle. Come, thy l'envoi begin.
Some enigma, some riddle. Come, begin your 'envoy', the poem's ending.
No egma, no riddle, no l'envoi, no salve in the mail, sir. O, sir, / plantain, a plain plantain! No l'envoi, no l'envoi, no salve, sir, / but a plantain.
No enigma, no riddle, no envoy, no ointment in the bag, sir. Oh, sir, a plantain leaf, a plain plantain! No envoy, no envoy, no ointment, sir, just a plantain.

By virtue, thou enforcest laughter; thy silly thought, my spleen; the / heaving of my lungs provokes me to ridiculous smiling. O, pardon me, my / stars! Doth the inconsiderate take salve for l'envoi, and the word / l'envoi for a salve?

Honestly, you force me to laugh; your silly idea forces my spleen; the heaving of my lungs makes me smile ridiculously. Oh, forgive me, my stars! Does this thoughtless fellow mistake 'salve' for 'envoy', and the word 'envoy' for a salve?
Do the wise think them other? Is not l'envoi a salve?
Do the wise think they're anything else? Isn't an envoy a salve (a farewell)?

No, page; it is an epilogue or discourse to make plain / Some obscure precedence that hath tofore been sain. / I will example it: / The fox, the ape, and the humble-bee / Were still at odds, being but three. / There's the moral. Now the l'envoi.

No, page; it's an epilogue or speech to explain something obscure that has been said before. I'll give an example: 'The fox, the ape and the bumble-bee were always at odds, being only three.' There's the moral. Now the envoy.
I will add the l'envoi. Say the moral again.
I'll add the envoy. Say the moral again.
The fox, the ape, and the humble-bee / Were still at odds, being but three.
'The fox, the ape and the bumble-bee were always at odds, being only three.'

Until the goose came out of door, / And stayed the odds by adding four. / Now will I begin your moral, and do you follow with my l'envoi. / The fox, the ape, and the humble-bee / Were still at odds, being but three.

'Until the goose came out of the door and settled the odds by making four.' Now I'll begin your moral, and you follow with my envoy. 'The fox, the ape and the bumble-bee were always at odds, being only three.'
Until the goose came out of door, / Staying the odds by adding four.
'Until the goose came out of the door, settling the odds by making four.'
A good l'envoi, ending in the goose. Would you desire more?
A good envoy, ending with the goose. What more could you want?

The boy hath sold him a bargain, a goose, that's flat. / Sir, your pennyworth is good, an your goose be fat. / To sell a bargain well is as cunning as fast and loose. / Let me see: a fat l'envoi—ay, that's a fat goose.

The boy has sold him a bargain, a goose (made a fool of him), that's for sure. Sir, you've got your money's worth, if your goose is fat. Selling a bargain well is as cunning a trick as 'fast and loose'. Let me see: a fat envoy; yes, that's a fat goose.
Come hither, come hither. How did this argument begin?
Come here, come here. How did this argument start?
By saying that a costard was broken in a shin. / Then called you for the l'envoi.
With my saying that a Costard had broken his shin. Then you called for the envoy.
True, and I for a plantain. Thus came your argument in. Then the boy's / fat l'envoi, the goose that you bought; and he ended the market.
True, and I called for a plantain. That's how your argument came in. Then the boy's fat envoy, the goose that you bought; and that closed the market.
But tell me, how was there a costard broken in a shin?
But tell me, how did a Costard break his shin?
I'll tell you so you can feel it.
Thou hast no feeling of it, Moth. I will speak that l'envoi. / I, Costard, running out, that was safely within, / Fell over the threshold and broke my shin.
You have no feeling of it, Moth. I'll speak that envoy. 'I, Costard, running out, when I was safely inside, fell over the doorstep and broke my shin.'
We will talk no more of this matter.
We'll say no more about this matter.
Till there be more matter in the shin.
Not till there's more matter (pus) in the shin.
Sirrah Costard, I will enfranchise thee.
Fellow Costard, I will enfranchise you.
O, marry me to one Frances! I smell some l'envoi, some goose, in / this.
Oh, marry me to some Frances! I smell some envoy, some goose (some trick), in this.
By my sweet soul, I mean setting thee at liberty, enfreedoming thy / person. Thou wert immured, restrained, captivated, bound.
By my sweet soul, I mean setting you at liberty, making your person free. You were walled up, restrained, captured, bound.
True, true; and now you will be my purgation, and let me loose.
True, true; and now you'll be my purge (my release) and let me loose.

I give thee thy liberty, set thee from durance, and, in lieu thereof, / impose on thee nothing but this: [Giving him a letter] bear this / significant to the country maid Jaquenetta. [Giving money] There is / remuneration for the best ward of mine honour is rewarding my / dependents. Moth, follow.

I give you your liberty, free you from imprisonment, and in return I ask nothing of you but this: [Giving him a letter] carry this message to the country girl Jaquenetta. [Giving money] There's a remuneration, for the best guard of my honour is rewarding my servants. Moth, follow.
Like the sequel, I. Signior Costard, adieu.
Like the sequel, I will. Signior Costard, goodbye.

My sweet ounce of man's flesh, my incony Jew! / Now will I look to his remuneration. "Remuneration"! O, that's the / Latin word for three farthings. Three farthings—remuneration. "What's / the price of this inkle?" "One penny." "No, I'll give you a / remuneration." Why, it carries it! Remuneration. Why, it is a fairer / name than French crown. I will never buy and sell out of this word.

My sweet ounce of man's flesh, my dainty jewel! Now let me look at his 'remuneration'. 'Remuneration'! Oh, that's the Latin word for three farthings. Three farthings: remuneration. 'What's the price of this tape?' 'One penny.' 'No, I'll give you a remuneration.' Why, that does the trick! Remuneration. Why, it's a finer name than a French crown. I'll never buy or sell without this word.
My good knave Costard, exceedingly well met.
My good fellow Costard, I'm very glad to meet you.
Pray you, sir, how much carnation ribbon may a man buy for a / remuneration?
Please, sir, how much pink ribbon can a man buy for a remuneration?
Why, sir, a halfpenny and a farthing.
Why, then, three-farthing worth of silk.
Why, then, three farthings' worth of silk.
I thank your worship. God be wi' you.
Thank you, your worship. God be with you.
Stay, slave. I must employ thee. / As thou wilt win my favour, good my knave, / Do one thing for me that I shall entreat.
Wait, fellow. I need you. If you want to win my favour, my good lad, do one thing I'll ask of you.
When would you have it done, sir?
When do you want it done, sir?
Well, I will do it, sir. Fare you well.
Well, I'll do it, sir. Goodbye.
Thou knowest not what it is.
You don't know what it is.
I shall know, sir, when I have done it.
I'll know, sir, when I've done it.
Why, villain, thou must know first.
Why, you rascal, you have to know first.
I will come to your worship tomorrow morning.
I'll come to your worship tomorrow morning.

It must be done this afternoon. Hark, slave, it is but this: / The Princess comes to hunt here in the park, / And in her train there is a gentle lady; / When tongues speak sweetly, then they name her name, / And Rosaline they call her. Ask for her / And to her white hand see thou do commend / This sealed-up counsel.

It has to be done this afternoon. Listen, fellow, it's only this. The Princess is coming to hunt here in the park, and among her attendants there's a gentle lady. When tongues speak sweetly, they say her name: they call her Rosaline. Ask for her, and make sure you deliver this sealed letter into her white hand.
Gardon, O sweet gardon! Better than remuneration, a 'levenpence / farthing better. Most sweet gardon! I will do it, sir, in print. / Gardon! Remuneration!
Reward, oh sweet reward! Better than remuneration: elevenpence-farthing better. Most sweet reward! I'll do it, sir, to the letter. Reward! Remuneration!

And I, forsooth, in love! I, that have been love's whip, / A very beadle to a humorous sigh, / A critic, nay, a night-watch constable, / A domineering pedant o'er the boy, / Than whom no mortal so magnificent! / This wimpled, whining, purblind, wayward boy, / This Signior Junior, giant-dwarf, Dan Cupid, / Regent of love-rhymes, lord of folded arms, / Th' anointed sovereign of sighs and groans, / Liege of all loiterers and malcontents, / Dread prince of plackets, king of codpieces, / Sole imperator, and great general / Of trotting paritors—O my little heart! / And I to be a corporal of his field / And wear his colours like a tumbler's hoop! / What? I love, I sue, I seek a wife? / A woman, that is like a German clock, / Still a-repairing, ever out of frame, / And never going aright, being a watch, / But being watched that it may still go right! / Nay, to be perjured, which is worst of all; / And, among three, to love the worst of all, / A whitely wanton with a velvet brow, / With two pitch-balls stuck in her face for eyes; / Ay, and, by heaven, one that will do the deed / Though Argus were her eunuch and her guard. / And I to sigh for her, to watch for her, / To pray for her! Go to, it is a plague / That Cupid will impose for my neglect / Of his almighty dreadful little might. / Well, I will love, write, sigh, pray, sue, and groan. / Some men must love my lady, and some Joan.

And I, of all people, in love! I, who have been love's whip, a real beadle punishing every fanciful sigh, a critic, no, a night-watchman, a bossy schoolmaster over the boy Cupid, than whom no mortal was more grand! This blindfolded, whining, half-blind, wilful boy, this Signior Junior, giant-dwarf, Lord Cupid, regent of love poems, lord of folded arms, the anointed king of sighs and groans, master of all idlers and malcontents, dread prince of petticoats, king of codpieces, sole emperor and great general of the officers who hunt down sexual sinners: oh my little heart! And I'm to be a corporal in his army and wear his colours like an acrobat's hoop! What? I love, I court, I look for a wife? A woman, who is like a German clock, always being repaired, always out of order, never running right however much it's a watch, unless it's watched to keep it going right! No, worse, to break my oath, which is worst of all; and, out of three, to love the worst of them: a pale, flirtatious girl with dark velvet brows and two balls of pitch stuck in her face for eyes; yes, and, by heaven, one who would do the deed even if hundred-eyed Argus were her eunuch and her guard. And I am to sigh for her, stay awake for her, pray for her! Come on, it's a punishment Cupid has given me for ignoring his almighty, dreadful little power. Well, I'll love, write, sigh, pray, plead and groan. Some men must love a lady, and some a Joan.
Was that the King that spurred his horse so hard / Against the steep uprising of the hill?
Was that the King who spurred his horse so hard up the steep slope of the hill?
I know not, but I think it was not he.
I don't know, but I don't think it was him.

Whoe'er he was, he showed a mounting mind. / Well, lords, today we shall have our dispatch; / On Saturday we will return to France. / Then, forester, my friend, where is the bush / That we must stand and play the murderer in?

Whoever he was, he showed an aspiring mind. Well, lords, today we'll have our business settled, and on Saturday we'll go back to France. Now, forester, my friend, where is the thicket where we must stand and play the murderer?
Hereby, upon the edge of yonder coppice, / A stand where you may make "the fairest shoot".
Close by, at the edge of that copse over there: a hiding place where you can make the fairest shot.
I thank my beauty, I am fair that shoot, / And thereupon thou speak'st the fairest shoot.
Thanks to my beauty, I am the fair one who shoots, and so you call it the 'fairest shoot'.
Pardon me, madam, for I meant not so.
Forgive me, madam, I didn't mean that.
What, what? First praise me, and again say no? / O short-lived pride! Not fair? Alack for woe!
What, what? First you praise me, and then say no? Oh, short-lived pride! Not fair? Alas, how sad!
Nay, never paint me now. / Where fair is not, praise cannot mend the brow. / Here, good my glass, take this for telling true:
No, don't paint me now. Where there's no beauty, praise can't improve a face. Here, my good mirror, take this for telling the truth:
Fair payment for foul words is more than due.
Fair payment for foul words is more than they deserve.
Nothing but fair is that which you inherit.
Everything you have is nothing but fair.

See, see, my beauty will be saved by merit. / O heresy in fair, fit for these days! / A giving hand, though foul, shall have fair praise. / But come, the bow. Now mercy goes to kill, / And shooting well is then accounted ill. / Thus will I save my credit in the shoot: / Not wounding, pity would not let me do't; / If wounding, then it was to show my skill, / That more for praise than purpose meant to kill. / And out of question so it is sometimes, / Glory grows guilty of detested crimes, / When, for fame's sake, for praise, an outward part, / We bend to that the working of the heart; / As I for praise alone now seek to spill / The poor deer's blood, that my heart means no ill.

Look, look, my beauty is saved by my good deeds! Oh, heresy about beauty, just right for these times! A hand that gives, however ugly, will get fair praise. But come, the bow. Now mercy goes out to kill, and shooting well counts as a bad thing. So I'll save my reputation in the hunt like this: if I don't wound the deer, it was pity that stopped me; if I do, it was to show my skill, and I aimed to kill more for praise than for any real purpose. And no doubt it is sometimes so: the love of glory becomes guilty of hateful crimes, when for fame's sake, for praise, which is only an outward thing, we bend the workings of our heart to it; as I now, only for praise, try to spill the poor deer's blood, though my heart means it no harm.
Do not curst wives hold that self-sovereignty / Only for praise' sake, when they strive to be / Lords o'er their lords?
Don't shrewish wives hold on to their self-rule just for praise, when they try to be lords over their lords?
Only for praise; and praise we may afford / To any lady that subdues a lord.
Only for praise; and we can give praise to any lady who conquers a lord.
Here comes a member of the commonwealth.
Here comes a member of the community.
God dig-you-den all! Pray you, which is the head lady?
God give you good evening, all! Please, which is the head lady?
Thou shalt know her, fellow, by the rest that have no heads.
You'll know her, fellow, because the rest have no heads.
Which is the greatest lady, the highest?
Which is the greatest lady, the highest?

The thickest and the tallest. It is so, truth is truth. / An your waist, mistress, were as slender as my wit, / One o' these maids' girdles for your waist should be fit. / Are not you the chief woman? You are the thickest here.

The thickest and the tallest. That's right; truth is truth. If your waist, mistress, were as slender as my wit, one of these girls' belts would fit you. Aren't you the chief woman? You're the thickest here.
What's your will, sir? What's your will?
What do you want, sir? What do you want?
I have a letter from Monsieur Berowne to one Lady Rosaline.
I have a letter from Monsieur Berowne to a Lady Rosaline.
O, thy letter, thy letter! He's a good friend of mine. / Stand aside, good bearer. Boyet, you can carve. / Break up this capon.
Oh, your letter, your letter! He's a good friend of mine. Stand aside, good messenger. Boyet, you can carve; cut up this chicken (open this letter).
I am bound to serve. / This letter is mistook; it importeth none here. / It is writ to Jaquenetta.
I'm bound to serve. This letter has been mixed up; it's for no one here. It's written to Jaquenetta.
We will read it, I swear. / Break the neck of the wax, and everyone give ear.
We'll read it, I swear. Break the seal, and everyone listen.

[Reads] By heaven, that thou art fair is most infallible; true that / thou art beauteous; truth itself that thou art lovely. More fairer than / fair, beautiful than beauteous, truer than truth itself, have / commiseration on thy heroical vassal. The magnanimous and most / illustrate King Cophetua set eye upon the pernicious and indubitate / beggar Zenelophon, and he it was that might rightly say, "Veni, vidi, / vici," which to annothanize in the vulgar—O base and obscure / vulgar!—videlicet, He came, see, and overcame. He came, one; see, / two; overcame, three. Who came? The King. Why did he come? To see. Why / did he see? To overcome. To whom came he? To the beggar. What saw he? / The beggar. Who overcame he? The beggar. The conclusion is victory. On / whose side? The King's. The captive is enriched. On whose side? The / beggar's. The catastrophe is a nuptial. On whose side? The King's? No, / on both in one, or one in both. I am the King, for so stands the / comparison; thou the beggar, for so witnesseth thy lowliness. Shall I / command thy love? I may. Shall I enforce thy love? I could. Shall I / entreat thy love? I will. What shalt thou exchange for rags? Robes. For / tittles? Titles. For thyself? Me. Thus expecting thy reply, I profane / my lips on thy foot, my eyes on thy picture, and my heart on thy every / part. / Thine in the dearest design of industry, / Don Adriano de Armado. / Thus dost thou hear the Nemean lion roar / 'Gainst thee, thou lamb, that standest as his prey. / Submissive fall his princely feet before, / And he from forage will incline to play. / But if thou strive, poor soul, what are thou then? / Food for his rage, repasture for his den.

[Reads] 'By heaven, it is utterly certain that you are fair; true that you are beautiful; the truth itself that you are lovely. More fairer than fair, more beautiful than beautiful, truer than truth itself, take pity on your heroic servant.
