The noble and most famous King Cophetua set eyes on the wicked and undoubted beggar Zenelophon, and he was the one who could rightly say, "Veni, vidi, vici", which to translate into the common tongue (oh, low and obscure common tongue!) is: he came, saw and conquered. He came, one; saw, two; conquered, three. Who came? The King. Why did he come? To see. Why did he see? To conquer. To whom did he come? To the beggar. What did he see? The beggar. Whom did he conquer? The beggar. The conclusion is victory: on whose side? The King's. The captive is made rich: on whose side? The beggar's. The final outcome is a wedding: on whose side? The King's? No, on both in one, or one in both. I am the King, for that is how the comparison goes; you are the beggar, as your lowliness shows. Shall I command your love? I may. Shall I force your love? I could. Shall I beg for your love? I will. What will you get in exchange for rags? Robes. For trifles? Titles. For yourself? Me. Expecting your reply, I kiss your foot with my lips, your picture with my eyes and every part of you with my heart. Yours in the most devoted plan of effort, Don Adriano de Armado.' 'So you hear the Nemean lion roar at you, little lamb, standing there as his prey. Fall humbly at his royal feet and he will turn from hunting to play. But if you struggle, poor soul, what are you then? Food for his rage and a meal for his den.'
What plume of feathers is he that indited this letter? / What vane? What weathercock? Did you ever hear better?
What feather-brained fop wrote this letter? What weather-vane? What weathercock? Did you ever hear anything better?
I am much deceived but I remember the style.
I'm much mistaken if I don't recognise the style.
Else your memory is bad, going o'er it erewhile.
Your memory must be bad otherwise, having just read through it.
This Armado is a Spaniard that keeps here in court, / A phantasime, a Monarcho, and one that makes sport / To the Prince and his book-mates.
This Armado is a Spaniard who lives here at court, a fantastic, a Monarcho (a famous mad braggart), who entertains the Prince and his fellow bookworms.
Thou, fellow, a word. / Who gave thee this letter?
You, fellow, a word. Who gave you this letter?
To whom shouldst thou give it?
Who were you supposed to give it to?
From my lord to my lady.
From my lord to my lady.
From which lord to which lady?
From which lord to which lady?
From my Lord Berowne, a good master of mine, / To a lady of France that he called Rosaline.
From my Lord Berowne, a good master of mine, to a French lady he called Rosaline.
Thou hast mistaken his letter. Come, lords, away. / Here, sweet, put up this: 'twill be thine another day.
You've delivered the wrong letter. Come, lords, let's go. Here, sweet, keep this; it'll be yours another day.
Who is the shooter? Who is the shooter?
Who is the shooter? Who is the shooter?
Shall I teach you to know?
Shall I teach you how to tell?
Why, she that bears the bow. / Finely put off!
Why, the one who carries the bow. Nicely dodged!
My lady goes to kill horns, but if thou marry, / Hang me by the neck if horns that year miscarry. / Finely put on!
My lady goes to kill horned deer; but if you marry, hang me if horns don't flourish that year (your husband will be a cuckold). Nicely hit!
Well, then, I am the shooter.
Well then, I am the shooter.
If we choose by the horns, yourself come not near. / Finely put on indeed!
If we choose by the horns, it's you; don't come near. A nice hit indeed!
You still wrangle with her, Boyet, and she strikes at the brow.
You keep squabbling with her, Boyet, and she aims at your forehead.
But she herself is hit lower. Have I hit her now?
But she herself is hit lower down. Have I hit her now?
Shall I come upon thee with an old saying, that was a man when King / Pepin of France was a little boy, as touching the hit it?
Shall I come at you with an old saying, which was already grown up when King Pepin of France was a little boy, about 'hitting it'?
So I may answer thee with one as old, that was a woman when Queen / Guinevere of Britain was a little wench, as touching the hit it.
Then I can answer with one just as old, which was a woman when Queen Guinevere of Britain was a little girl, about 'hitting it'.
Thou canst not hit it, hit it, hit it, / Thou canst not hit it, my good man.
(Singing) You can't hit it, hit it, hit it, you can't hit it, my good man.
An I cannot, cannot, cannot, / An I cannot, another can.
(Singing) And if I can't, can't, can't, if I can't, another man can.
By my troth, most pleasant. How both did fit it!
Honestly, very pleasant. How well they both matched it!
A mark marvellous well shot, for they both did hit it.
A target wonderfully well shot, because they both hit it.
A mark! O, mark but that mark! A mark, says my lady! / Let the mark have a prick in't, to mete at, if it may be.
A target! Just look at that target! A target, says my lady! Let the target have a bullseye in it to aim at, if possible.
Wide o' the bow hand! I' faith, your hand is out.
Wide on the left! Really, you're out of practice.
Indeed, a' must shoot nearer, or he'll ne'er hit the clout.
Yes, he must shoot closer, or he'll never hit the middle.
An if my hand be out, then belike your hand is in.
And if I'm out of practice, then perhaps you're in.
Then will she get the upshoot by cleaving the pin.
Then she'll win the match by splitting the peg in the centre.
Come, come, you talk greasily, your lips grow foul.
Come on, you're talking dirty; your lips are getting foul.
She's too hard for you at pricks, sir. Challenge her to bowl.
She's too good for you at archery, sir. Challenge her to bowls.
I fear too much rubbing. Good night, my good owl.
I'm afraid of too much rubbing. Good night, my good owl.

By my soul, a swain, a most simple clown! / Lord, Lord, how the ladies and I have put him down! / O' my troth, most sweet jests, most incony vulgar wit, / When it comes so smoothly off, so obscenely, as it were, so fit. / Armado, o' the one side, O, a most dainty man! / To see him walk before a lady and to bear her fan! / To see him kiss his hand and how most sweetly he will swear! / And his page o' t'other side, that handful of wit! / Ah, heavens, it is a most pathetical nit.

By my soul, a peasant, a most simple clown! Lord, Lord, how the ladies and I put him down! Honestly, very sweet jokes, very fine, common wit, when it comes off so smoothly, so obscenely, as it were, so neatly. Armado on one side: oh, a very dainty man! To see him walk in front of a lady and carry her fan! To see him kiss his hand, and how sweetly he swears! And his page on the other side, that handful of wit! Ah, heavens, he is a most moving little flea.
Very reverend sport, truly, and done in the testimony of a good / conscience.
Very respectable sport, truly, and done with a clear conscience.

The deer was, as you know, sanguis, in blood, ripe as the pomewater, / who now hangeth like a jewel in the ear of caelo, the sky, the / welkin, the heaven, and anon falleth like a crab on the face of / terra, the soil, the land, the earth.

The deer was, as you know, 'sanguis', in prime condition, ripe as an apple, which hangs now like a jewel in the ear of 'caelo', the sky, the heavens, the firmament, and in a moment falls like a crab-apple on the face of 'terra', the soil, the land, the earth.
Truly, Master Holofernes, the epithets are sweetly varied, like a / scholar at the least. But, sir, I assure ye it was a buck of the first / head.

Truly, Master Holofernes, your descriptive words are sweetly varied, like a scholar's at the very least. But, sir, I assure you it was a buck of the first head (a five-year-old deer with its first full antlers).
Sir Nathaniel, 'haud credo': I don't believe it.
'Twas not a "auld grey doe", 'twas a pricket.
It wasn't an 'old grey doe'; it was a pricket (a two-year-old buck).

Most barbarous intimation! Yet a kind of insinuation, as it were, in / via, in way, of explication; facere, as it were, replication, or / rather, ostentare, to show, as it were, his inclination, after his / undressed, unpolished, uneducated, unpruned, untrained, or rather, / unlettered, or ratherest, unconfirmed fashion, to insert again my haud / credo for a deer.

A most barbarous suggestion! Yet a kind of hint, as it were, 'in via', on the way to explaining; 'facere', as it were, a reply; or rather 'ostentare', to show, as it were, his inclination, in his undressed, unpolished, uneducated, unpruned, untrained, or rather unlettered, or rather-est, unconfirmed way, to put in again my 'haud credo' for a deer.
I said the deer was not a "auld grey doe", 'twas a pricket.
I said the deer wasn't an 'old grey doe'; it was a pricket.
Twice-sod simplicity, bis coctus! / O, thou monster Ignorance, how deformed dost thou look!
Twice-boiled stupidity, 'bis coctus'! Oh, you monster Ignorance, how deformed you look!

Sir, he hath never fed of the dainties that are bred of a book. / He hath not eat paper, as it were; he hath not drunk ink. / His intellect is not replenished; he is only an animal, only sensible / in the duller parts. / And such barren plants are set before us that we thankful should be— / Which we of taste and feeling are—for those parts that do fructify in / us more than he. / For as it would ill become me to be vain, indiscreet, or a fool, / So, were there a patch set on learning, to see him in a school. / But, omne bene, say I, being of an old father's mind; / Many can brook the weather that love not the wind.

Sir, he has never fed on the delicacies that grow in books. He hasn't eaten paper, so to speak; he hasn't drunk ink. His mind isn't nourished; he's only an animal, with feeling only in his duller parts. And such barren plants are set before us so that we, who have taste and feeling, should be thankful for the parts in us that bear more fruit than his. For just as it would be wrong for me to be vain, foolish or a fool, it would be like patching a fool onto learning to see him in a school. But 'omne bene', all's well, I say, agreeing with an old Church Father: many can stand the weather who don't like the wind.
You two are bookmen. Can you tell me by your wit / What was a month old at Cain's birth, that's not five weeks old as yet?
You two are bookmen. Can you tell me, with your cleverness, what was a month old when Cain was born, and isn't five weeks old yet?
Dictynna, goodman Dull. Dictynna, goodman Dull.
Dictynna, goodman Dull. Dictynna, goodman Dull.
A title to Phoebe, to Luna, to the moon.
A name for Phoebe, for Luna, for the moon.
The moon was a month old when Adam was no more, / And raught not to five weeks when he came to five-score. / Th' allusion holds in the exchange.
The moon was a month old when Adam was no older, and hadn't reached five weeks when he reached a hundred. The allusion holds good when you swap the names.
'Tis true, indeed. The collusion holds in the exchange.
That's true, indeed. The collusion holds good in the exchange.
God comfort thy capacity! I say, th' allusion holds in the exchange.
God help your brain! I said, the allusion holds good in the exchange.
And I say the pollution holds in the exchange, for the moon is never / but a month old; and I say beside that 'twas a pricket that the / Princess killed.
And I say the pollution holds good in the exchange, because the moon is never more than a month old; and what's more, I say it was a pricket that the Princess killed.
Sir Nathaniel, will you hear an extemporal epitaph on the death of the / deer? And, to humour the ignorant, call I the deer the Princess killed / a pricket.
Sir Nathaniel, will you hear an improvised epitaph on the death of the deer? And, to humour the ignorant, I'll call the deer the Princess killed a pricket.
Perge, good Master Holofernes, perge, so it shall please you to / abrogate scurrility.
'Perge', go on, good Master Holofernes, go on, as long as you leave out anything rude.

I will something affect the letter; for it argues facility. / The preyful Princess pierced and pricked a pretty pleasing pricket; / Some say a sore; but not a sore till now made sore with shooting. / The dogs did yell, put "l" to sore, then sorel jumps from thicket; / Or pricket sore, or else sorel, the people fall a-hooting. / If sore be sore, then "L" to "sore" makes fifty sores o' sorel. / Of one sore I an hundred make, by adding but one more "L".

I'll indulge in a little alliteration, for it shows fluency. 'The predatory Princess pierced and pricked a pretty, pleasing pricket. Some say a sore (a four-year-old buck), but it wasn't sore until shooting made it sore. The dogs yelled; put "L" on "sore" and a sorel (a three-year-old buck) jumps out of the thicket; whether pricket, sore or sorel, the people start shouting. If sore is sore, then L (fifty in Roman numerals) added to sore makes fifty sores of sorel. From one sore I make a hundred, by adding just one more L.'
[Aside] If a talent be a claw, look how he claws him with a talent.
[Aside] If a talent is a talon (a claw), see how he claws at him with flattery.

This is a gift that I have, simple, simple; a foolish extravagant / spirit, full of forms, figures, shapes, objects, ideas, apprehensions, / motions, revolutions. These are begot in the ventricle of memory, / nourished in the womb of pia mater, and delivered upon the mellowing / of occasion. But the gift is good in those in whom it is acute, and I / am thankful for it.

This is a gift I have, simple, simple: a foolish, wandering spirit, full of forms, figures, shapes, objects, ideas, notions, impulses, changes. They are conceived in the chamber of memory, nourished in the womb of the brain and born when the moment is ripe. But the gift is good in those in whom it is sharp, and I am thankful for it.
Sir, I praise the Lord for you, and so may my parishioners, for their / sons are well tutored by you, and their daughters profit very greatly / under you. You are a good member of the commonwealth.
Sir, I praise the Lord for you, and so may my parishioners, because their sons are well taught by you, and their daughters do very well under you. You're a fine member of the community.
Mehercle! If their sons be ingenious, they shall want no instruction; / if their daughters be capable, I will put it to them. But, vir sapit / qui pauca loquitur. A soul feminine saluteth us.

By Hercules! If their sons are clever, they'll lack no instruction; if their daughters are able, I'll put it to them. But 'vir sapit qui pauca loquitur': the wise man speaks little. A female soul greets us.
God give you good morrow, Master Person.
God give you good morning, Master Parson.
Master Person, quasi pierce one. And if one should be pierced, which / is the one?
Master 'Person', as if 'pierce-one'. And if one were to be pierced, which is the one?
Marry, Master schoolmaster, he that is likest to a hogshead.
Why, Master Schoolmaster, the one most like a barrel.
Of piercing a hogshead! A good lustre or conceit in a turf of earth; / fire enough for a flint, pearl enough for a swine. 'Tis pretty; it is / well.
Of piercing a barrel! A good spark of wit in a lump of earth; enough fire for a flint, a pearl good enough for a pig. It's pretty; it's well done.
Good Master Parson, be so good as read me this letter. It was given me / by Costard, and sent me from Don Armado. I beseech you read it.
Good Master Parson, please be so kind as to read me this letter. Costard gave it to me, and Don Armado sent it. Please read it.

Fauste precor, gelida quando pecus omne sub umbra Ruminat— / and so forth. Ah, good old Mantuan, I may speak of thee as the / traveller doth of Venice: / Venetia, Venetia, / Chi non ti vede, non ti pretia. / Old Mantuan, old Mantuan! Who understandeth thee not, loves thee not. / [He sings] / Ut, re, sol, la, mi, fa. / Under pardon, sir, what are the contents? Or rather as Horace says in / his—What, my soul, verses?

'Fauste, precor, gelida quando pecus omne sub umbra ruminat' (a line from the Latin poet Mantuan), and so on. Ah, good old Mantuan, I can say of you what the traveller says of Venice: 'Venice, Venice, whoever does not see you does not prize you.' Old Mantuan, old Mantuan! Whoever doesn't understand you doesn't love you. [He sings] Do, re, so, la, mi, fa. With your pardon, sir, what does it say? Or rather, as Horace says in his... What, my soul, verses?
Yes, sir, and very learned ones.
Let me hear a staff, a stanze, a verse, / Lege, domine.
Let me hear a stanza, a stanza, a verse. 'Lege, domine': read, sir.

[Reads] / If love make me forsworn, how shall I swear to love? / Ah, never faith could hold, if not to beauty vowed. / Though to myself forsworn, to thee I'll faithful prove. / Those thoughts to me were oaks, to thee like osiers bowed. / Study his bias leaves, and makes his book thine eyes, / Where all those pleasures live that art would comprehend. / If knowledge be the mark, to know thee shall suffice. / Well learned is that tongue that well can thee commend, / All ignorant that soul that sees thee without wonder; / Which is to me some praise, that I thy parts admire. / Thy eye Jove's lightning bears, thy voice his dreadful thunder, / Which, not to anger bent, is music and sweet fire. / Celestial as thou art, O, pardon love this wrong, / That sings heaven's praise with such an earthly tongue.

[Reads] 'If love makes me break my oath, how can I swear to love? Ah, no promise could ever hold unless it was made to beauty. Though I break faith with myself, I'll be faithful to you. Those vows that were like oaks to me bend like willows before you. The student leaves his course and makes your eyes his book, where all the pleasures live that learning wants to grasp. If knowledge is the target, knowing you will be enough. Well-educated is the tongue that can praise you well; utterly ignorant the soul that sees you without wonder; and it is some credit to me that I admire your qualities. Your eye carries Jove's lightning, your voice his dreadful thunder, which, when not meant in anger, is music and sweet fire. Heavenly as you are, oh, forgive love this wrong, that sings heaven's praise with such an earthly tongue.'

You find not the apostrophus, and so miss the accent. Let me supervise / the canzonet. [He takes the letter] Here are only numbers ratified, / but, for the elegancy, facility, and golden cadence of poesy, caret. / Ovidius Naso was the man. And why indeed "Naso," but for smelling out / the odoriferous flowers of fancy, the jerks of invention? Imitari is / nothing: so doth the hound his master, the ape his keeper, the tired / horse his rider. But, damosella virgin, was this directed to you?

You don't observe the apostrophes, and so you miss the stresses. Let me look over the little song. [He takes the letter] There's nothing here but metre in order; as for the elegance, fluency and golden rhythm of poetry, 'caret', it's missing. Ovidius Naso was the man. And why indeed 'Naso' (nose), except for smelling out the sweet-scented flowers of fancy, the flashes of invention? 'Imitari', imitating, is nothing: the dog does that to his master, the ape to his keeper, the harnessed horse to his rider. But, 'damosella', virgin, was this addressed to you?
Ay, sir, from one Monsieur Berowne, one of the strange queen's lords.
Yes, sir, from a Monsieur Berowne, one of the foreign queen's lords.

I will overglance the superscript: To the snow-white hand of the most / beauteous Lady Rosaline. I will look again on the intellect of the / letter, for the nomination of the party writing to the person written / unto: Your Ladyship's in all desired employment, Berowne. Sir / Nathaniel, this Berowne is one of the votaries with the King, and here / he hath framed a letter to a sequent of the stranger queen's, which / accidentally, or by the way of progression, hath miscarried. Trip and / go, my sweet, deliver this paper into the royal hand of the King. It / may concern much. Stay not thy compliment. I forgive thy duty. Adieu.

I'll glance at the address: 'To the snow-white hand of the most beautiful Lady Rosaline.' I'll look again at the content of the letter for the name of the person writing to the person written to: 'Your Ladyship's in all desired service, Berowne.' Sir Nathaniel, this Berowne is one of the men under oath with the King, and here he has written a letter to a follower of the foreign queen, which accidentally, or on its way, has gone astray. Off you go, my sweet; deliver this paper into the King's royal hand. It may be very important. Don't stay to curtsy. I excuse you from your duty. Goodbye.
Good Costard, go with me. Sir, God save your life.
Good Costard, come with me. Sir, God save your life.
Sir, you have done this in the fear of God, very religiously; and, as a / certain Father saith—
Sir, you've done this in the fear of God, very religiously; and, as a certain Church Father says...
Sir, tell not me of the Father, I do fear colourable colours. But to / return to the verses: did they please you, Sir Nathaniel?
Sir, don't tell me about the Fathers; I'm wary of plausible excuses. But to come back to the verses: did you like them, Sir Nathaniel?

I do dine today at the father's of a certain pupil of mine, where if, / before repast, it shall please you to gratify the table with a grace, I / will, on my privilege I have with the parents of the foresaid child or / pupil, undertake your ben venuto; where I will prove those verses to / be very unlearned, neither savouring of poetry, wit, nor invention. I / beseech your society.

I'm dining today at the house of the father of a certain pupil of mine, where, if you would like to grace the table by saying grace before the meal, I will, on the strength of my standing with the parents of that child or pupil, guarantee your welcome. There I'll prove those verses to be very unlearned, tasting of neither poetry, wit nor invention. I'd be glad of your company.
And thank you too; for society, saith the text, is the happiness of / life.
And thank you too; for company, the text says, is the happiness of life.
And certes, the text most infallibly concludes it. [To Dull] Sir, I / do invite you too. You shall not say me nay. Pauca verba. Away! The / gentles are at their game, and we will to our recreation.

And truly, the text concludes it beyond any doubt. [To Dull] Sir, I invite you too. You shan't say no to me. 'Pauca verba': few words. Let's go! The gentry are at their sport, and we'll go to our entertainment.

The King, he is hunting the deer; I am coursing myself. They have / pitched a toil; I am toiling in a pitch, pitch that defiles. Defile! A / foul word! Well, set thee down, sorrow, for so they say the fool said, / and so say I, and I the fool. Well proved, wit! By the Lord, this love / is as mad as Ajax. It kills sheep, it kills me, I a sheep. Well proved / again, o' my side! I will not love; if I do, hang me! I' faith, I will / not. O, but her eye! By this light, but for her eye, I would not love / her; yes, for her two eyes. Well, I do nothing in the world but lie, / and lie in my throat. By heaven, I do love, and it hath taught me to / rhyme, and to be melancholy. And here is part of my rhyme, and here my / melancholy. Well, she hath one o' my sonnets already. The clown bore / it, the fool sent it, and the lady hath it. Sweet clown, sweeter fool, / sweetest lady! By the world, I would not care a pin if the other three / were in. Here comes one with a paper. God give him grace to groan!

The King is hunting the deer; I'm hunting myself. They have set up a net; I'm struggling in pitch, pitch that soils. Soil! A dirty word! Well, 'sit down, sorrow', as they say the fool said; and so say I, and I'm the fool. Well argued, wit! By the Lord, this love is as mad as Ajax: it kills sheep; it kills me, and I'm a sheep. Well argued again, on my side! I won't love; if I do, hang me! Honestly, I won't. Oh, but her eye! By this light, if it weren't for her eye, I wouldn't love her; yes, for her two eyes. Well, I do nothing in the world but lie, and lie through my teeth. By heaven, I do love, and it has taught me to rhyme and to be melancholy; and here is part of my rhyme, and here is my melancholy. Well, she has one of my sonnets already. The clown carried it, the fool sent it and the lady has it. Sweet clown, sweeter fool, sweetest lady! By the world, I wouldn't care a pin if the other three were in love too. Here comes one with a paper. God give him the grace to groan!
[Aside] Shot, by heaven! Proceed, sweet Cupid, thou hast thumped him / with thy birdbolt under the left pap. In faith, secrets!
[Aside] Hit, by heaven! Carry on, sweet Cupid; you've thumped him with your blunt arrow under the left nipple. Honestly, secrets!

[Reads] / So sweet a kiss the golden sun gives not / To those fresh morning drops upon the rose, / As thy eye-beams, when their fresh rays have smote / The night of dew that on my cheeks down flows. / Nor shines the silver moon one half so bright / Through the transparent bosom of the deep / As doth thy face, through tears of mine give light. / Thou shin'st in every tear that I do weep. / No drop but as a coach doth carry thee; / So ridest thou triumphing in my woe. / Do but behold the tears that swell in me, / And they thy glory through my grief will show. / But do not love thyself; then thou wilt keep / My tears for glasses, and still make me weep. / O queen of queens, how far dost thou excel / No thought can think, nor tongue of mortal tell. / How shall she know my griefs? I'll drop the paper. / Sweet leaves, shade folly. Who is he comes here?

[Reads] 'The golden sun doesn't give as sweet a kiss to the fresh morning dewdrops on the rose as your eyes' rays give when their fresh beams strike the night's dew of tears that runs down my cheeks. And the silver moon doesn't shine half as brightly through the clear depths of the sea as your face, shining through my tears. You shine in every tear I weep. Every drop carries you like a coach, so you ride in triumph through my sorrow. Just look at the tears that well up in me, and they'll show your glory through my grief. But don't fall in love with yourself; then you'd keep my tears as mirrors and make me weep for ever. Oh queen of queens, no thought can think and no mortal tongue can tell how far you surpass all others.' How will she know my griefs? I'll drop the paper. Sweet leaves, hide my foolishness. Who's this coming?
What, Longaville, and reading! Listen, ear.
What, Longaville, and reading! Listen, ear.
[Aside] Now, in thy likeness, one more fool appear!
[Aside] Now, dressed just like you, here comes one more fool!
Oh dear! I have broken my oath.
Why, he comes in like a perjure, wearing papers.
Why, he comes in like a perjurer, wearing papers (as perjurers were made to wear, listing their crime).
In love, I hope. Sweet fellowship in shame.
In love, I hope. Sweet companionship in shame.
One drunkard loves another of the name.
One drunkard loves another of the same kind.
Am I the first that have been perjured so?
Am I the first to have broken his oath like this?
I could put thee in comfort: not by two that I know. / Thou makest the triumviry, the corner-cap of society, / The shape of love's Tyburn, that hangs up simplicity.
I could comfort you: not by two that I know of. You make up the threesome, the three-cornered cap of our company, the shape of love's Tyburn gallows, that hangs up simple-mindedness.
I fear these stubborn lines lack power to move. / O sweet Maria, empress of my love, / These numbers will I tear, and write in prose.
I'm afraid these stiff lines aren't moving enough. Oh sweet Maria, empress of my love, I'll tear up these verses and write in prose.
O, rhymes are guards on wanton Cupid's hose. / Disfigure not his shop.
Oh, rhymes are the trimmings on wanton Cupid's trousers. Don't spoil his merchandise.

Did not the heavenly rhetoric of thine eye, / 'Gainst whom the world cannot hold argument, / Persuade my heart to this false perjury? / Vows for thee broke deserve not punishment. / A woman I forswore, but I will prove, / Thou being a goddess, I forswore not thee. / My vow was earthly, thou a heavenly love; / Thy grace being gained, cures all disgrace in me. / Vows are but breath, and breath a vapour is. / Then thou, fair sun, which on my earth dost shine, / Exhal'st this vapour-vow; in thee it is. / If broken then, it is no fault of mine; / If by me broke, what fool is not so wise / To lose an oath to win a paradise?

'Didn't the heavenly eloquence of your eyes, which the whole world can't argue against, persuade my heart to this false perjury? Vows broken for you don't deserve punishment. I gave up women, but I'll prove that since you're a goddess, I didn't give up you. My vow was earthly; you are a heavenly love. Winning your grace cures all my disgrace. Vows are only breath, and breath is only vapour. So you, fair sun, shining on my earth, draw up this vapour-vow; it lives in you. If it's broken, then, it isn't my fault; and if I did break it, what fool isn't wise enough to lose an oath to win paradise?'
This is the liver vein, which makes flesh a deity, / A green goose a goddess. Pure, pure idolatry. / God amend us, God amend! We are much out o' th' way.

This is the passionate vein (the liver was thought the seat of love), which makes flesh into a god and a silly goose into a goddess. Pure, pure idolatry. God help us, God help us! We've gone badly astray.
By whom shall I send this?—Company! Stay.
Who can I send this with? Someone's coming! Wait.

All hid, all hid, an old infant play. / Like a demigod here sit I in the sky, / And wretched fools' secrets heedfully o'er-eye. / More sacks to the mill. O heavens, I have my wish. / Dumaine transformed! Four woodcocks in a dish!

All hide, all hide: an old children's game. Like a demigod I sit up here in the sky and carefully watch wretched fools' secrets. More sacks to the mill! Oh heavens, I have my wish: Dumaine transformed! Four fools in one dish!
By heaven, the wonder in a mortal eye!
By heaven, the wonder in a mortal eye!
By earth, she is but corporal. There you lie.
By earth, she's only flesh and blood. There you lie.
Her amber hairs for foul hath amber quoted.
Her amber hair has shown that amber is ugly by comparison.
An amber-coloured raven was well noted.
Stoop, I say. / Her shoulder is with child.
Bending, I'd say. Her shoulder is pregnant (she's hunched).
Ay, as some days, but then no sun must shine.
Yes, as some days, but ones when the sun doesn't shine.
O, that I had my wish!
Oh, if only I had my wish!
And I mine too, good Lord!
And I mine too, good Lord!
Amen, so I had mine. Is not that a good word?
Amen, if I had mine. Isn't that a good word?
I would forget her; but a fever she / Reigns in my blood, and will remembered be.
I'd like to forget her; but she rules in my blood like a fever and won't be forgotten.
A fever in your blood? Why, then incision / Would let her out in saucers. Sweet misprision!
A fever in your blood? Why, then, cutting a vein would let her out into bowls. A sweet mistake!
Once more I'll read the ode that I have writ.
I'll read the poem I've written once more.
Once more I'll mark how love can vary wit.
I'll watch once more how love can vary a man's wits.

[Dumaine reads his sonnet] / On a day—alack the day!— / Love, whose month is ever May, / Spied a blossom passing fair / Playing in the wanton air. / Through the velvet leaves the wind, / All unseen, can passage find; / That the lover, sick to death, / Wished himself the heaven's breath. / "Air," quoth he, "thy cheeks may blow; / Air, would I might triumph so!" / But, alack, my hand is sworn / Ne'er to pluck thee from thy thorn. / Vow, alack, for youth unmeet, / Youth so apt to pluck a sweet. / Do not call it sin in me, / That I am forsworn for thee; / Thou for whom Jove would swear / Juno but an Ethiope were, / And deny himself for Jove, / Turning mortal for thy love. / This will I send, and something else more plain, / That shall express my true love's fasting pain. / O, would the King, Berowne and Longaville / Were lovers too! Ill, to example ill, / Would from my forehead wipe a perjured note, / For none offend where all alike do dote.

[Dumaine reads his sonnet] 'One day (alas, that day!) Love, whose month is always May, saw a beautiful blossom playing in the wanton air. Through the velvet leaves, unseen, the wind found a way in, so that the lover, sick to death, wished he were the breath of heaven. "Air," he said, "you may blow on her cheeks; Air, I wish I could triumph like you!" But, alas, my hand has sworn never to pluck you from your thorn: a vow, alas, unfit for youth, which is so ready to pluck sweetness. Don't call it a sin in me that I break my oath for you, you for whom Jove would swear that Juno is ugly as an Ethiopian, and would deny he was Jove, turning mortal for your love.' I'll send this, and something else plainer that will express the pain of my true love's starving. Oh, if only the King, Berowne and Longaville were in love too! Others' bad example would wipe the mark of a perjurer off my forehead, for no one is guilty where everyone dotes alike.
[Comes forward] Dumaine, thy love is far from charity, / That in love's grief desir'st society. / You may look pale, but I should blush, I know, / To be o'erheard and taken napping so.
[Comes forward] Dumaine, your love is far from charity, wanting company in love's grief. You may look pale, but I know I'd blush to be overheard and caught out like this.

[Comes forward] Come, sir, you blush. As his, your case is such. / You chide at him, offending twice as much. / You do not love Maria? Longaville / Did never sonnet for her sake compile, / Nor never lay his wreathed arms athwart / His loving bosom to keep down his heart. / I have been closely shrouded in this bush, / And marked you both, and for you both did blush. / I heard your guilty rhymes, observed your fashion, / Saw sighs reek from you, noted well your passion. / "Ay, me!" says one. "O Jove!" the other cries. / One, her hairs were gold; crystal the other's eyes. / [To Longaville] You would for paradise break faith and troth; / [To Dumaine] And Jove, for your love would infringe an oath. / What will Berowne say when that he shall hear / Faith infringed which such zeal did swear? / How will he scorn, how will he spend his wit! / How will he triumph, leap, and laugh at it! / For all the wealth that ever I did see, / I would not have him know so much by me.

[Comes forward] Come, sir, you blush. Your case is just like his. You scold him, while you're twice as guilty. You don't love Maria? Longaville never wrote a sonnet for her sake, never folded his arms across his loving chest to hold down his heart? I've been hidden closely in this bush and watched you both, and blushed for you both. I heard your guilty rhymes, watched how you behaved, saw sighs steam out of you, noted your passion well. 'Oh dear!' says one. 'Oh Jove!' cries the other. One says her hair is gold; the other that her eyes are crystal. [To Longaville] You'd break your faith and word for paradise; [To Dumaine] and Jove would break an oath for your love. What will Berowne say when he hears about a promise broken that was sworn so passionately? How he'll mock, how he'll spend his wit on it! How he'll triumph, jump about and laugh at it! For all the riches I've ever seen, I wouldn't want him to know as much about me.

[Comes forward] / Now step I forth to whip hypocrisy. / Ah, good my liege, I pray thee pardon me. / Good heart, what grace hast thou thus to reprove / These worms for loving, that art most in love? / Your eyes do make no coaches; in your tears / There is no certain princess that appears. / You'll not be perjured, 'tis a hateful thing: / Tush, none but minstrels like of sonneting! / But are you not ashamed? Nay, are you not, / All three of you, to be thus much o'ershot? / You found his mote, the King your mote did see; / But I a beam do find in each of three. / O, what a scene of foolery have I seen, / Of sighs, of groans, of sorrow, and of teen! / O me, with what strict patience have I sat, / To see a king transformed to a gnat! / To see great Hercules whipping a gig, / And profound Solomon to tune a jig, / And Nestor play at push-pin with the boys, / And critic Timon laugh at idle toys. / Where lies thy grief, O, tell me, good Dumaine? / And, gentle Longaville, where lies thy pain? / And where my liege's? All about the breast? / A caudle, ho!

[Comes forward] Now I step out to whip hypocrisy. Ah, my good lord, forgive me, please. Good heart, what right have you to scold these worms for loving, when you're the most in love of all? Your eyes don't make coaches; no particular princess appears in your tears. You won't break your oath; it's a hateful thing. Pah, only minstrels like writing sonnets! But aren't you ashamed? No, aren't you all three ashamed to be so caught out? You found the speck in his eye, the King saw the speck in yours; but I find a plank in each of the three. Oh, what a scene of foolishness I've watched, of sighs, groans, sorrow and suffering! Oh my, with what strict patience I have sat to see a king turned into a gnat, to see great Hercules spinning a top, and wise Solomon singing a jig, and old Nestor playing children's games with the boys, and the scornful Timon laughing at silly toys! Where is your grief? Oh, tell me, good Dumaine. And, gentle Longaville, where is your pain? And where is my lord's? All around the heart? A hot drink for the sick, quickly!
Too bitter is thy jest. / Are we betrayed thus to thy over-view?
Your joke is too bitter. Have we been given away like this to your spying?

Not you to me, but I betrayed by you. / I that am honest, I that hold it sin / To break the vow I am engaged in. / I am betrayed by keeping company / With men like you, men of inconstancy. / When shall you see me write a thing in rhyme? / Or groan for Joan? Or spend a minute's time / In pruning me? When shall you hear that I / Will praise a hand, a foot, a face, an eye, / A gait, a state, a brow, a breast, a waist, / A leg, a limb—

Not you to me, but I betrayed by you. I, who am honest, who think it a sin to break the vow I'm bound by, am betrayed by keeping company with men like you, inconstant men. When will you ever see me write anything in rhyme? Or groan for some Joan? Or spend a minute prettying myself up? When will you hear me praise a hand, a foot, a face, an eye, a walk, a bearing, a brow, a breast, a waist, a leg, a limb...
Soft! Whither away so fast? / A true man, or a thief, that gallops so?
Wait! Where are you off to so fast? Is it an honest man or a thief who gallops like that?
I post from love. Good lover, let me go.
I'm running away from love. Good lover, let me go.
What gift have you got there?
If it mar nothing neither, / The treason and you go in peace away together.
If it isn't undoing anything either, then the treason and you can go away in peace together.
I beseech your Grace, let this letter be read. / Our person misdoubts it; 'twas treason, he said.
Please, Your Grace, have this letter read. Our parson suspects it; he said it was treason.
How now, what is in you? Why dost thou tear it?
What's the matter with you? Why are you tearing it?
A toy, my liege, a toy. Your Grace needs not fear it.
It's a trifle, my lord, a trifle. Your Grace needn't worry about it.
It did move him to passion, and therefore let's hear it.
It made him very upset, so let's hear it.
[Picking up the pieces] / It is Berowne's writing, and here is his name.
[Picking up the pieces] It's Berowne's handwriting, and here's his name.
[To Costard] Ah, you whoreson loggerhead, you were born to do me / shame. / Guilty, my lord, guilty. I confess, I confess.
[To Costard] Ah, you bastard blockhead, you were born to disgrace me. Guilty, my lord, guilty. I confess, I confess.

That you three fools lacked me fool to make up the mess. / He, he, and you—and you, my liege—and I / Are pick-purses in love, and we deserve to die. / O, dismiss this audience, and I shall tell you more.

That you three fools needed me, a fool, to make up the set of four. He, he and you (and you, my lord) and I are pickpockets in love, and we deserve to die. Oh, send these people away and I'll tell you more.
True, true, we are four. / Will these turtles be gone?
True, true, we are four. Will these lovebirds go?
Walk aside the true folk, and let the traitors stay.
Let the honest folk walk away, and let the traitors stay.

Sweet lords, sweet lovers, O, let us embrace! / As true we are as flesh and blood can be. / The sea will ebb and flow, heaven show his face; / Young blood doth not obey an old decree. / We cannot cross the cause why we were born; / Therefore of all hands must we be forsworn.

Sweet lords, sweet lovers, oh, let's embrace! We're as true as flesh and blood can be. The sea will ebb and flow, the sky show its face; young blood doesn't obey an old decree. We can't go against the reason we were born; so, whichever way we turn, we must break our oaths.
What, did these rent lines show some love of thine?
What, did these torn lines show some love of yours?

"Did they?" quoth you? Who sees the heavenly Rosaline / That, like a rude and savage man of Ind, / At the first op'ning of the gorgeous east, / Bows not his vassal head and, strucken blind, / Kisses the base ground with obedient breast? / What peremptory eagle-sighted eye / Dares look upon the heaven of her brow / That is not blinded by her majesty?

'Did they?' you ask? Who can see the heavenly Rosaline and not, like a rough savage from India at the first opening of the gorgeous dawn, bow his humble head and, struck blind, kiss the lowly ground with an obedient chest? What bold, eagle-eyed eye dares to look at the heaven of her brow and not be blinded by her majesty?
What zeal, what fury hath inspired thee now? / My love, her mistress, is a gracious moon; / She, an attending star, scarce seen a light.
What passion, what frenzy has inspired you now? My love, her mistress, is a gracious moon; she's an attending star, barely seen as a light.

My eyes are then no eyes, nor I Berowne. / O, but for my love, day would turn to night! / Of all complexions the culled sovereignty / Do meet as at a fair in her fair cheek, / Where several worthies make one dignity, / Where nothing wants that want itself doth seek. / Lend me the flourish of all gentle tongues— / Fie, painted rhetoric! O, she needs it not. / To things of sale a seller's praise belongs. / She passes praise; then praise too short doth blot. / A withered hermit, five-score winters worn, / Might shake off fifty, looking in her eye. / Beauty doth varnish age, as if new born, / And gives the crutch the cradle's infancy. / O, 'tis the sun that maketh all things shine!

Then my eyes aren't eyes, and I'm not Berowne. Oh, if it weren't for my love, day would turn to night! The pick of all the best complexions meet in her fair cheek as if at a fair, where many good qualities make one perfection, where nothing is lacking that desire itself could want. Lend me the decoration of every fine tongue... No, away with painted rhetoric! Oh, she doesn't need it. A seller's praise belongs to things for sale. She is beyond praise; so praise that falls short only stains her. A withered hermit, worn by a hundred winters, could shake off fifty of them by looking in her eyes. Beauty varnishes old age as if it were newborn, and gives the man on crutches the childhood of the cradle. Oh, she is the sun that makes everything shine!
By heaven, thy love is black as ebony.
By heaven, your love is as black as ebony.

Is ebony like her? O word divine! / A wife of such wood were felicity. / O, who can give an oath? Where is a book? / That I may swear beauty doth beauty lack / If that she learn not of her eye to look. / No face is fair that is not full so black.

Is ebony like her? Oh, divine word! A wife made of such wood would be bliss. Oh, who can give an oath? Where's a Bible? So that I can swear that beauty lacks beauty unless it learns how to look from her eyes. No face is fair that isn't just as black.
O paradox! Black is the badge of hell, / The hue of dungeons and the school of night; / And beauty's crest becomes the heavens well.
Oh, what a paradox! Black is the badge of hell, the colour of dungeons and the gown of night; and beauty's true emblem is the bright sky.

Devils soonest tempt, resembling spirits of light. / O, if in black my lady's brows be decked, / It mourns that painting and usurping hair / Should ravish doters with a false aspect; / And therefore is she born to make black fair. / Her favour turns the fashion of the days, / For native blood is counted painting now; / And therefore red, that would avoid dispraise, / Paints itself black, to imitate her brow.

Devils tempt soonest when they look like spirits of light. Oh, if my lady's brows are dressed in black, it's because they mourn that make-up and false hair should seduce fools with a fake appearance; and so she was born to make black beautiful. Her looks change the fashion of the times, for natural colour is now thought to be paint; and so red cheeks, to avoid criticism, paint themselves black to imitate her brow.
To look like her are chimney-sweepers black.
Chimney sweeps are black to look like her.
And since her time are colliers counted bright.
And since she came along, coal-miners are counted handsome.
And Ethiopes of their sweet complexion crack.
And Ethiopians boast of their lovely complexion.
Dark needs no candles now, for dark is light.
Darkness doesn't need candles now, because dark is light.
Your mistresses dare never come in rain, / For fear their colours should be washed away.
Your mistresses never dare go out in the rain, for fear their colours would be washed off.
'Twere good yours did; for, sir, to tell you plain, / I'll find a fairer face not washed today.
It would be good if yours did; for, sir, to be honest, I'll find a fairer face that hasn't been washed today.
I'll prove her fair, or talk till doomsday here.
I'll prove she's fair, or talk here until doomsday.
No devil will fright thee then so much as she.
Then no devil will frighten you as much as she does.
I never knew man hold vile stuff so dear.
I never knew a man to value such poor stuff so highly.
[Showing his shoe] / Look, here's thy love, my foot and her face see.
[Showing his shoe] Look, here's your love: see my foot and her face (both black).
O, if the streets were paved with thine eyes, / Her feet were much too dainty for such tread.
Oh, if the streets were paved with your eyes, her feet would be too dainty to tread on them.
O vile! Then, as she goes, what upward lies / The street should see as she walked over head.
Oh, how vile! Then, as she walked, the street would see what's up under her skirts.
But what of this? Are we not all in love?
But what of all this? Aren't we all in love?
Nothing so sure, and thereby all forsworn.
Nothing is surer, and so we've all broken our oaths.
Then leave this chat, and, good Berowne, now prove / Our loving lawful, and our faith not torn.
Then leave this chatter, and, good Berowne, prove now that our loving is lawful and our faith is not broken.
Ay, marry, there; some flattery for this evil.
Yes indeed, that's it; some flattering excuse for this evil.
O, some authority how to proceed. / Some tricks, some quillets, how to cheat the devil.
Oh, some authority to tell us how to go on; some tricks, some quibbles, to cheat the devil.

O, 'tis more than need. / Have at you, then, affection's men-at-arms. / Consider what you first did swear unto: / To fast, to study, and to see no woman— / Flat treason 'gainst the kingly state of youth. / Say, can you fast? Your stomachs are too young, / And abstinence engenders maladies. / O, we have made a vow to study, lords, / And in that vow we have forsworn our books; / For when would you, my liege, or you, or you, / In leaden contemplation have found out / Such fiery numbers as the prompting eyes / Of beauty's tutors have enriched you with? / Other slow arts entirely keep the brain, / And therefore, finding barren practisers, / Scarce show a harvest of their heavy toil; / But love, first learned in a lady's eyes, / Lives not alone immured in the brain, / But with the motion of all elements / Courses as swift as thought in every power, / And gives to every power a double power, / Above their functions and their offices. / It adds a precious seeing to the eye. / A lover's eyes will gaze an eagle blind. / A lover's ear will hear the lowest sound, / When the suspicious head of theft is stopped. / Love's feeling is more soft and sensible / Than are the tender horns of cockled snails. / Love's tongue proves dainty Bacchus gross in taste. / For valour, is not Love a Hercules, / Still climbing trees in the Hesperides? / Subtle as Sphinx, as sweet and musical / As bright Apollo's lute, strung with his hair. / And when Love speaks, the voice of all the gods / Make heaven drowsy with the harmony. / Never durst poet touch a pen to write / Until his ink were tempered with Love's sighs. / O, then his lines would ravish savage ears / And plant in tyrants mild humility. / From women's eyes this doctrine I derive. / They sparkle still the right Promethean fire; / They are the books, the arts, the academes, / That show, contain, and nourish, all the world; / Else none at all in aught proves excellent. / Then fools you were these women to forswear, / Or, keeping what is sworn, you will prove fools. / For wisdom's sake, a word that all men love, / Or for love's sake, a word that loves all men, / Or for men's sake, the authors of these women, / Or women's sake, by whom we men are men, / Let us once lose our oaths to find ourselves, / Or else we lose ourselves to keep our oaths. / It is religion to be thus forsworn, / For charity itself fulfils the law, / And who can sever love from charity?

Oh, there's more than enough. Here goes, then, love's soldiers. Think what you first swore to do: to fast, to study and to see no woman. That's outright treason against the royal state of youth. Tell me, can you fast? Your stomachs are too young, and going without breeds diseases. Oh, we made a vow to study, lords, and in that vow we gave up our real books. For when would you, my lord, or you, or you, in dull, leaden thinking, ever have come up with such fiery verses as the inspiring eyes of beauty's tutors have given you? Other slow kinds of learning stay entirely in the brain, and so, finding barren students, hardly show a harvest for their heavy work. But love, first learned in a lady's eyes, doesn't live shut up in the brain alone. It moves as fast as thought through every faculty, like the elements, and gives each faculty double power, beyond its normal work. It adds precious sight to the eye: a lover's eyes can outstare an eagle. A lover's ear can hear the faintest sound, when even a suspicious thief hears nothing. Love's touch is softer and more sensitive than the tender horns of snails. Love's tongue makes dainty Bacchus seem crude in his taste. For courage, isn't Love a Hercules, still climbing trees in the garden of the Hesperides? It is as subtle as the Sphinx, as sweet and musical as bright Apollo's lute strung with his golden hair. And when Love speaks, the voices of all the gods make heaven drowsy with their harmony. No poet ever dared to touch a pen to write until his ink was mixed with Love's sighs; oh, then his lines would enchant savage ears and plant gentle humility in tyrants. This is the lesson I draw from women's eyes. They always sparkle with the true fire of Prometheus; they are the books, the arts, the academies that show, contain and nourish the whole world. Without them, no one is excellent at anything. So you were fools to give up these women, and if you keep your oath you'll prove yourselves fools. For wisdom's sake, a word all men love; or for love's sake, a word that loves all men; or for men's sake, who made these women; or for women's sake, who make us men: let's lose our oaths once to find ourselves, or else we lose ourselves to keep our oaths. It is a religious act to break our oaths like this; for love itself fulfils the law, and who can separate love from charity?
Saint Cupid, then, and, soldiers, to the field!
Then Saint Cupid, and to the battlefield, soldiers!
Advance your standards, and upon them, lords! / Pell-mell, down with them! But be first advised / In conflict that you get the sun of them.
Raise your banners, and at them, lords! Charge, down with them! But make sure first that in the fight you get the sun behind you (in their eyes).
Now to plain dealing. Lay these glozes by. / Shall we resolve to woo these girls of France?
Now let's talk plainly. Put these fine glosses aside. Shall we resolve to woo these girls from France?
And win them too. Therefore let us devise / Some entertainment for them in their tents.
And win them too. So let's plan some entertainment for them in their tents.

First, from the park let us conduct them thither. / Then homeward every man attach the hand / Of his fair mistress. In the afternoon / We will with some strange pastime solace them, / Such as the shortness of the time can shape; / For revels, dances, masques, and merry hours / Forerun fair Love, strewing her way with flowers.

First let's escort them there from the park. Then on the way home let each man take the hand of his fair mistress. In the afternoon we'll entertain them with some unusual amusement, as much as the short time allows; for revels, dances, masques and merry hours go in front of fair Love, scattering flowers in her path.
Away, away! No time shall be omitted / That will betime and may by us be fitted.
Away, away! We won't waste a moment of the time we have that can be used.
Allons! allons! Sowed cockle reaped no corn, / And justice always whirls in equal measure. / Light wenches may prove plagues to men forsworn; / If so, our copper buys no better treasure.

Let's go! Let's go! Sow weeds and you don't reap corn, and justice always turns around fairly. Loose girls may turn out to be a plague to men who break their oaths; if so, our copper coins buy no better treasure.
'Satis quod sufficit': enough is as good as a feast.

I praise God for you, sir. Your reasons at dinner have been sharp and / sententious, pleasant without scurrility, witty without affection, / audacious without impudency, learned without opinion, and strange / without heresy. I did converse this quondam day with a companion of / the King's, who is intituled, nominated, or called, Don Adriano de / Armado.

I praise God for you, sir. Your conversation at dinner has been sharp and full of wise sayings, pleasant without being rude, witty without being affected, bold without being impudent, learned without being opinionated, and original without being heretical. The other day I was talking with a companion of the King's, who is entitled, named or called Don Adriano de Armado.

Novi hominem tanquam te. His humour is lofty, his discourse / peremptory, his tongue filed, his eye ambitious, his gait majestical / and his general behaviour vain, ridiculous, and thrasonical. He is too / picked, too spruce, too affected, too odd, as it were, too peregrinate, / as I may call it.

'Novi hominem tanquam te': I know the man as well as I know you. His manner is lofty, his speech overbearing, his tongue polished, his eye ambitious, his walk majestic and his general behaviour vain, ridiculous and boastful. He is too refined, too spruce, too affected, too odd, as it were, too much the traveller, as I might call it.
A most singular and choice epithet.
A most remarkable and choice description.

He draweth out the thread of his verbosity finer than the staple of his / argument. I abhor such fanatical phantasimes, such insociable and / point-devise companions, such rackers of orthography, as to speak / "dout" sine "b", when he should say "doubt", "det" when he should / pronounce "debt"—d, e, b, t, not d, e, t. He clepeth a calf "cauf", / half "hauf"; neighbour vocatur "nebour", neigh abbreviated "ne". This / is abhominable, which he would call "abominable". It insinuateth me of / insanie. Ne intelligis, domine? To make frantic, lunatic.

He draws out the thread of his wordiness finer than the substance of his argument. I loathe such fantastic weirdos, such unsociable and over-precise fellows, such torturers of spelling, who say 'dout' without the 'b' when he should say 'doubt', and 'det' when he should pronounce 'debt': d, e, b, t, not d, e, t. He calls a calf a 'cauf', half 'hauf'; 'neighbour' he calls 'nebour', and 'neigh' is shortened to 'ne'. This is abhominable (which he would call 'abominable'). It drives me to insanie. 'Ne intelligis, domine?' Do you understand, sir? To make frantic, lunatic.
'Laus Deo, bone intelligo': praise God, I understand well.
Bone? Bone for bene? Priscian a little scratched; 'twill serve.
'Bone'? 'Bone' for 'bene'? Priscian's grammar is a little scratched; it'll do.
'Videsne quis venit?' Do you see who's coming?
'Video, et gaudeo': I see, and rejoice.
Chirrah! (He means the Greek greeting 'chaire', or mispronounces 'sirrah'.)
[Aside to Costard] They have been at a great feast of languages and / stolen the scraps.
[Aside to Costard] They've been at a great feast of languages and stolen the leftovers.

O, they have lived long on the almsbasket of words. I marvel thy master / hath not eaten thee for a word, for thou art not so long by the head as / honorificabilitudinitatibus. Thou art easier swallowed than a / flap-dragon.

Oh, they've lived for a long time on the scrap basket of words. I'm amazed your master hasn't eaten you up for a word, because you're not as long from head to foot as 'honorificabilitudinitatibus'. You'd be easier to swallow than a flaming raisin in a drinking game.
Quiet! The bells are starting to ring.
[To Holofernes] Monsieur, are you not lettered?
Yes, yes, he teaches boys the hornbook. What is a, b, spelt backward / with the horn on his head?
Yes, yes, he teaches boys their alphabet. What is 'a, b' spelt backwards, with a horn on its head?
Ba, pueritia, with a horn added.
Ba, most silly sheep with a horn. You hear his learning.
'Baa', you very silly sheep with a horn. You hear how learned he is.
'Quis, quis', who, who, you consonant (you nobody)?
The third of the five vowels, if you repeat them; or the fifth, if I.
The third of the five vowels, if you say them; or the fifth, if I do.
I will repeat them: a, e, i—
I'll say them: a, e, I...
The sheep. The other two concludes it: o, u.
The sheep (you're the ewe, the 'I'). The other two finish it: o, u (oh, you).
Now, by the salt wave of the Mediterraneum, a sweet touch, a quick / venue of wit! Snip, snap, quick and home! It rejoiceth my intellect. / True wit!
Now, by the salty waves of the Mediterranean, a sweet touch, a quick fencing hit of wit! Snip, snap, quick and right on target! It delights my intellect. True wit!
Offered by a child to an old man—which is wit-old.
Offered by a child to an old man, which is 'wit-old' (wittol: a willing cuckold).
What is the figure? What is the figure?
What's the figure of speech? What's the figure?
Thou disputes like an infant. Go whip thy gig.
You argue like a baby. Go and spin your top.
Lend me your horn to make one, and I will whip about your infamy unum / cita. A gig of a cuckold's horn.
Lend me your horn to make one, and I'll whip your shame around 'unum cita' (he means 'circum circa', round and round). A top made of a cuckold's horn!

An I had but one penny in the world, thou shouldst have it to buy / gingerbread. Hold, there is the very remuneration I had of thy master, / thou halfpenny purse of wit, thou pigeon-egg of discretion. O, an the / heavens were so pleased that thou wert but my bastard, what a joyful / father wouldst thou make me! Go to, thou hast it ad dunghill, at the / fingers' ends, as they say.

If I had only one penny in the world, you'd have it to buy gingerbread. Here, there's the very remuneration I got from your master, you halfpenny purse of wit, you pigeon's egg of good sense. Oh, if heaven had made you my bastard, what a happy father you'd make me! Go on, you have it 'ad dunghill', at your fingertips, as they say.
O, I smell false Latin! Dunghill for unguem.
Oh, I smell bad Latin! 'Dunghill' for 'unguem' (ad unguem: to a fingernail, perfectly).
Arts-man, preambulate. We will be singuled from the barbarous. Do you / not educate youth at the charge-house on the top of the mountain?
Man of learning, walk ahead. We will separate ourselves from the barbarians. Don't you teach young people at the school on the top of the mountain?
At your sweet pleasure, for the mountain.
Sir, it is the King's most sweet pleasure and affection to congratulate / the Princess at her pavilion in the posteriors of this day, which the / rude multitude call the afternoon.
Sir, it is the King's sweet pleasure and wish to pay his respects to the Princess at her pavilion in the posteriors of this day, which the rough masses call the afternoon.
The posterior of the day, most generous sir, is liable, congruent, and / measurable for the afternoon. The word is well culled, chose, sweet, / and apt, I do assure you, sir, I do assure.
The posterior of the day, most noble sir, is suitable, fitting and appropriate for the afternoon. The word is well picked, chosen, sweet and apt, I assure you, sir, I assure you.

Sir, the King is a noble gentleman, and my familiar, I do assure ye, / very good friend. For what is inward between us, let it pass. I do / beseech thee, remember thy courtesy; I beseech thee, apparel thy head. / And among other importunate and most serious designs, and of great / import indeed, too—but let that pass. For I must tell thee it will / please his Grace, by the world, sometime to lean upon my poor shoulder / and with his royal finger thus dally with my excrement, with my / mustachio. But, sweet heart, let that pass. By the world, I recount no / fable! Some certain special honours it pleaseth his greatness to impart / to Armado, a soldier, a man of travel, that hath seen the world. But / let that pass. The very all of all is—but, sweet heart, I do implore / secrecy—that the King would have me present the Princess, sweet chuck, / with some delightful ostentation, or show, or pageant, or antic, or / firework. Now, understanding that the curate and your sweet self are / good at such eruptions and sudden breaking-out of mirth, as it were, I / have acquainted you withal, to the end to crave your assistance.

Sir, the King is a noble gentleman and an intimate friend of mine, I assure you, a very good friend. As for what is private between us, let it pass. I beg you, remember your courtesy; I beg you, put your hat back on. And among other pressing and very serious plans, and of great importance indeed... but let that pass. For I must tell you, it pleases His Grace, by the world, sometimes to lean on my poor shoulder and play with my excrement, that is, my moustache, with his royal finger, like this. But, sweetheart, let that pass. By the world, I am not telling tales! It pleases His Greatness to grant some special honours to Armado, a soldier, a traveller, who has seen the world. But let that pass. The be-all and end-all is (but, sweetheart, I beg you to keep it secret) that the King wants me to present the Princess, sweet chick, with some delightful display, or show, or pageant, or comic dance, or fireworks. Now, knowing that the curate and your sweet self are good at such eruptions and sudden outbursts of fun, as it were, I have told you about it in order to ask your help.

Sir, you shall present before her the Nine Worthies. Sir Nathaniel, as / concerning some entertainment of time, some show in the posterior of / this day, to be rendered by our assistance, the King's command, and / this most gallant, illustrate, and learned gentleman, before the / Princess, I say, none so fit as to present the Nine Worthies.

Sir, you shall present the Nine Worthies before her. Sir Nathaniel, as for some entertainment, some show in the posterior of this day, to be performed with our help, at the King's command and by this most gallant, famous and learned gentleman, before the Princess: I say nothing is as fitting as to present the Nine Worthies.
Where will you find men worthy enough to present them?
Where will you find men worthy enough to play them?
Joshua, yourself; myself; and this gallant gentleman, Judas Maccabaeus. / This swain, because of his great limb or joint, shall pass Pompey the / Great; the page, Hercules.
Joshua, yourself; myself, and this gallant gentleman, Judas Maccabaeus; this peasant, because of his big limbs and joints, will pass for Pompey the Great; the page, Hercules.
Pardon, sir; error. He is not quantity enough for that Worthy's thumb; / he is not so big as the end of his club.
Excuse me, sir: error. He isn't big enough for that Worthy's thumb; he isn't as big as the end of his club.
Shall I have audience? He shall present Hercules in minority. His enter / and exit shall be strangling a snake; and I will have an apology for / that purpose.
May I be heard? He will play Hercules as a child. His entrance and exit will show him strangling a snake, and I'll have an explanatory speech for the purpose.

An excellent device! So, if any of the audience hiss, you may cry "Well / done, Hercules, now thou crushest the snake!" That is the way to make / an offence gracious, though few have the grace to do it.

An excellent plan! Then if anyone in the audience hisses, you can shout, 'Well done, Hercules, now you're crushing the snake!' That's the way to make an offence look graceful, though few have the grace to do it.
For the rest of the Worthies?
And the rest of the Worthies?
Shall I tell you a thing?
We will have, if this fadge not, an antic. I beseech you, follow.
If this doesn't work, we'll have a comic dance. Please, follow me.
Via, goodman Dull! Thou has spoken no word all this while.
Come on, goodman Dull! You haven't said a word all this time.
Let's go! We'll give you a part.
I'll make one in a dance, or so; or I will play on the tabor to the / Worthies, and let them dance the hay.
I'll join in a dance, or something; or I'll play the drum for the Worthies and let them dance a country dance.
Most dull, honest Dull! To our sport, away.
Most dull, honest Dull! To our entertainment, away.
Sweet hearts, we shall be rich ere we depart, / If fairings come thus plentifully in. / A lady walled about with diamonds! / Look you what I have from the loving King.
Sweethearts, we'll be rich before we leave if presents keep coming in like this. A lady walled in with diamonds! Look what I've had from the loving King.
Madam, came nothing else along with that?
Madam, didn't anything else come with it?
Nothing but this? Yes, as much love in rhyme / As would be crammed up in a sheet of paper / Writ o' both sides the leaf, margent and all, / That he was fain to seal on Cupid's name.
Nothing but this? Yes, as much love in rhyme as could be crammed onto a sheet of paper, written on both sides, margins and all, so that he had to seal it on Cupid's name.
That was the way to make his godhead wax, / For he hath been five thousand years a boy.
That was the way to make the god grow bigger (as wax), because he has been a boy for five thousand years.
Ay, and a shrewd unhappy gallows too.
Yes, and a nasty, mischievous rascal too.
You'll ne'er be friends with him. He killed your sister.
You'll never be friends with him. He killed your sister.

He made her melancholy, sad, and heavy; / And so she died. Had she been light, like you, / Of such a merry, nimble, stirring spirit, / She might ha' been a grandam ere she died. / And so may you, for a light heart lives long.

He made her melancholy, sad and heavy-hearted, and so she died. If she had been light like you, with such a merry, nimble, lively spirit, she might have been a grandmother before she died. And so may you, because a light heart lives long.
What's your dark meaning, mouse, of this light word?
What's your dark meaning, little mouse, in this light word?
A light condition in a beauty dark.
A light (wanton) character in a dark beauty.
We need more light to find your meaning out.
We need more light to work out your meaning.
You'll mar the light by taking it in snuff; / Therefore I'll darkly end the argument.
You'll spoil the light by taking it in snuff (taking offence, like a smoking candle-wick); so I'll end the argument in the dark.
Look what you do, you do it still i' th' dark.
Whatever you do, you always do it in the dark.
So do not you, for you are a light wench.
You don't, because you're a light girl.
Indeed, I weigh not you, and therefore light.
It's true, I don't weigh you, and so I'm light.
You weigh me not? O, that's you care not for me.
You don't weigh me? Oh, that means you don't care about me.
Great reason, for past cure is still past care.
With good reason, because what's past cure is past care.
Well bandied both; a set of wit well played. / But, Rosaline, you have a favour too. / Who sent it? And what is it?
Well volleyed, both of you; a set of wit well played. But Rosaline, you have a present too. Who sent it? And what is it?

I would you knew. / An if my face were but as fair as yours, / My favour were as great. Be witness this. / Nay, I have verses too, I thank Berowne; / The numbers true, and, were the numbering too, / I were the fairest goddess on the ground. / I am compared to twenty thousand fairs. / O, he hath drawn my picture in his letter.

I wish you knew. If my face were as fair as yours, my present would be as great. Look at this. No, I have verses too, thanks to Berowne. The metre is correct, and if the measuring of me were correct too, I'd be the fairest goddess on earth. I'm compared to twenty thousand beauties. Oh, he's drawn my portrait in his letter.
Much in the letters, nothing in the praise.
Very like in the letters (black ink), nothing like in the praise.
Beauteous as ink: a good conclusion.
As beautiful as ink: a good conclusion.
Fair as a text B in a copy-book.
As fair as a black capital B in a copybook.
'Ware pencils, how! Let me not die your debtor, / My red dominical, my golden letter. / O, that your face were not so full of O's!
Watch out for paintbrushes, there! I won't die in your debt, my red Sunday letter in the calendar, my gilded letter. Oh, if only your face weren't so full of O's (pockmarks)!
A pox of that jest! And beshrew all shrews. / But, Katharine, what was sent to you from fair Dumaine?
A plague on that joke! And curse all shrews. But, Katharine, what did fair Dumaine send you?
Did he not send you twain?
Yes, madam, and moreover, / Some thousand verses of a faithful lover. / A huge translation of hypocrisy, / Vilely compiled, profound simplicity.
Yes, madam, and on top of that, some thousand verses of a faithful lover: a huge translation of hypocrisy, wretchedly put together, deeply simple-minded.
This, and these pearls, to me sent Longaville. / The letter is too long by half a mile.
Longaville sent this to me, and these pearls. The letter is too long by half a mile.
I think no less. Dost thou not wish in heart / The chain were longer and the letter short?
I quite believe it. Don't you wish in your heart that the chain were longer and the letter short?
Ay, or I would these hands might never part.
Yes, or I wish these hands might never part.
We are wise girls to mock our lovers so.
We're clever girls, to mock our lovers like this.

They are worse fools to purchase mocking so. / That same Berowne I'll torture ere I go. / O that I knew he were but in by th' week! / How I would make him fawn, and beg, and seek, / And wait the season, and observe the times, / And spend his prodigal wits in bootless rhymes, / And shape his service wholly to my hests, / And make him proud to make me proud that jests! / So pair-taunt-like would I o'ersway his state, / That he should be my fool, and I his fate.

They're worse fools, to buy mockery at such a price. That Berowne, I'll torture him before I leave. Oh, if only I knew he was trapped for good! How I would make him fawn and beg and seek, and wait for the right season and keep to the right times, and waste his extravagant wits on useless rhymes, and shape all his service to my orders, and make him proud to make me proud, who only jest! I'd rule over his life so like a fateful planet that he would be my fool, and I his fate.
None are so surely caught, when they are catched, / As wit turned fool. Folly, in wisdom hatched, / Hath wisdom's warrant and the help of school / And wit's own grace to grace a learned fool.
No one is so firmly caught, once caught, as wit turned fool. Folly hatched in a wise man has wisdom's authority, the help of education and wit's own grace to grace a learned fool.
The blood of youth burns not with such excess / As gravity's revolt to wantonness.
The blood of youth doesn't burn as fiercely as seriousness when it rebels into wantonness.
Folly in fools bears not so strong a note / As fool'ry in the wise when wit doth dote, / Since all the power thereof it doth apply / To prove, by wit, worth in simplicity.
Folly in fools is not as striking as foolishness in the wise when their wit dotes, since it uses all its power to prove, by wit, that silliness is worthwhile.
Here comes Boyet, and mirth is in his face.
Here comes Boyet, with laughter in his face.
O, I am stabbed with laughter! Where's her Grace?
Oh, I'm stabbed with laughter! Where's Her Grace?

Prepare, madam, prepare! / Arm, wenches, arm! Encounters mounted are / Against your peace. Love doth approach disguised, / Armed in arguments. You'll be surprised. / Muster your wits, stand in your own defence, / Or hide your heads like cowards, and fly hence.

Get ready, madam, get ready! To arms, girls, to arms! An attack is being mounted against your peace. Love is coming in disguise, armed with arguments. You'll be ambushed. Gather your wits, stand and defend yourselves, or hide your heads like cowards and run away.
Saint Denis to Saint Cupid! What are they / That charge their breath against us? Say, scout, say.
Saint Denis against Saint Cupid! Who are they who aim their breath at us? Speak, scout, speak.

Under the cool shade of a sycamore / I thought to close mine eyes some half an hour, / When, lo, to interrupt my purposed rest, / Toward that shade I might behold addressed / The King and his companions. Warily / I stole into a neighbour thicket by, / And overheard what you shall overhear: / That, by and by, disguised they will be here. / Their herald is a pretty knavish page / That well by heart hath conned his embassage. / Action and accent did they teach him there: / "Thus must thou speak," and "thus thy body bear." / And ever and anon they made a doubt / Presence majestical would put him out; / "For," quoth the King, "an angel shalt thou see; / Yet fear not thou, but speak audaciously." / The boy replied "An angel is not evil; / I should have feared her had she been a devil." / With that all laughed and clapped him on the shoulder, / Making the bold wag by their praises bolder. / One rubbed his elbow thus, and fleered, and swore / A better speech was never spoke before. / Another with his finger and his thumb / Cried "Via, we will do 't, come what will come." / The third he capered, and cried "All goes well!" / The fourth turned on the toe, and down he fell. / With that they all did tumble on the ground, / With such a zealous laughter, so profound, / That in this spleen ridiculous appears, / To check their folly, passion's solemn tears.

I was thinking of closing my eyes for half an hour in the cool shade of a sycamore, when, look, to interrupt my rest, I saw the King and his companions heading towards that shade. Carefully I crept into a thicket nearby and overheard what you're about to hear: that very soon they'll come here in disguise. Their messenger is a pretty, rascally page who has learned his message by heart. They were teaching him gestures and delivery there: 'This is how you must speak', and 'this is how you hold yourself'. And every so often they worried that a majestic presence would make him forget his lines. 'For,' said the King, 'you'll see an angel; but don't be afraid, speak out boldly.' The boy answered, 'An angel isn't evil; I'd have been afraid of her if she'd been a devil.' At that they all laughed and clapped him on the shoulder, making the cheeky boy bolder with their praise. One rubbed his elbow like this, grinned and swore a better speech had never been spoken. Another snapped his finger and thumb and cried, 'Come on, we'll do it, come what may.' The third danced about and cried, 'All's going well!' The fourth spun on his toe and fell over. At that they all tumbled on the ground with such hearty, deep laughter that in this fit of silliness solemn tears of emotion appeared, to check their folly.
But what, but what, come they to visit us?
But what, but what? Are they coming to visit us?

They do, they do, and are apparelled thus, / Like Muscovites, or Russians, as I guess. / Their purpose is to parley, court, and dance, / And every one his love-feat will advance / Unto his several mistress, which they'll know / By favours several which they did bestow.

They are, they are, and they're dressed like this: as Muscovites, or Russians, I'd guess. They plan to talk, court and dance, and each one will press his love-suit on his own mistress, whom they'll recognise by the different presents they sent.

And will they so? The gallants shall be tasked; / For, ladies, we will every one be masked, / And not a man of them shall have the grace, / Despite of suit, to see a lady's face. / Hold, Rosaline, this favour thou shalt wear, / And then the King will court thee for his dear. / Hold, take thou this, my sweet, and give me thine, / So shall Berowne take me for Rosaline. / And change you favours too; so shall your loves / Woo contrary, deceived by these removes.

Will they really? These gallants shall be put to the test. For, ladies, we'll all be masked, and not one of them will be allowed, however much he begs, to see a lady's face. Here, Rosaline, you wear this present, and then the King will court you as his darling. Here, my sweet, take this, and give me yours; then Berowne will take me for Rosaline. And you two swap presents too; then your lovers, deceived by these exchanges, will woo the wrong ladies.
Come on, then, wear the favours most in sight.
Come on, then, wear the presents where they can be seen.
But in this changing, what is your intent?
But what do you mean by this swapping?

The effect of my intent is to cross theirs. / They do it but in mocking merriment, / And mock for mock is only my intent. / Their several counsels they unbosom shall / To loves mistook, and so be mocked withal / Upon the next occasion that we meet, / With visages displayed to talk and greet.

What I mean by it is to cross their plan. They're only doing it as a mocking joke, and all I intend is mockery for mockery. They'll pour out their secret feelings to the wrong ladies, and so be mocked for it the next time we meet them, with our faces showing, to talk and greet.
But shall we dance, if they desire us to't?
But shall we dance if they want us to?
No, to the death we will not move a foot, / Nor to their penned speech render we no grace, / But while 'tis spoke each turn away her face.
No, not for our lives will we move a foot, and we won't honour their prepared speech either; while it's spoken, each of us will turn her face away.
Why, that contempt will kill the speaker's heart, / And quite divorce his memory from his part.
Why, that contempt will break the speaker's heart and make him forget his part completely.
