Therefore I do it, and I make no doubt / The rest will ne'er come in, if he be out. / There's no such sport as sport by sport o'erthrown, / To make theirs ours and ours none but our own. / So shall we stay, mocking intended game, / And they, well mocked, depart away with shame.

That's why I'm doing it; and I've no doubt the rest will never come in if he dries up. There's no sport like sport overthrown by sport: making their game ours and keeping ours to ourselves. So we'll stay, mocking the game they planned, and they, well mocked, will leave in shame.
The trumpet sounds. Be masked; the maskers come.
The trumpet sounds. Put on your masks; the masquers are coming.
All hail, the richest beauties on the earth!
All hail, the richest beauties on the earth!
Beauties no richer than rich taffeta.
Beauties no richer than rich silk (their masks).
A holy parcel of the fairest dames
A holy group of the fairest ladies
That ever turned their—backs—to mortal views!
that ever turned their... backs... to mortal eyes!
Their eyes, you rogue, their eyes.
That ever turned their eyes to mortal views. / Out—
that ever turned their eyes to mortal eyes. Out...
True; he's out (forgotten his lines) indeed.
Out of your favours, heavenly spirits, vouchsafe / Not to behold—
Out of your kindness, heavenly spirits, please do not look...
Once to behold with your sun-beamed eyes— / With your sun-beamed eyes—
please do look with your sun-bright eyes... with your sun-bright eyes...
They will not answer to that epithet. / You were best call it "daughter-beamed eyes".
They won't answer to that description. You'd better call them 'daughter-bright eyes'.
They do not mark me, and that brings me out.
They're not paying attention to me, and that's putting me off.
Is this your perfectness? Be gone, you rogue!
Is this how well you know it? Get out, you rogue!
What would these strangers? Know their minds, Boyet. / If they do speak our language, 'tis our will / That some plain man recount their purposes. / Know what they would.
What do these strangers want? Find out what they mean, Boyet. If they speak our language, we wish some plain man to tell us their purpose. Find out what they want.
What would you with the Princess?
What do you want with the Princess?
Nothing but peace and gentle visitation.
Nothing but peace and a polite visit.
What do they say they want?
Nothing but peace and gentle visitation.
Nothing but peace and a polite visit.
Why, that they have, and bid them so be gone.
Why, they've had that, so tell them to go.
She says you have it, and you may be gone.
She says you've had it, and you may go.
Say to her we have measured many miles / To tread a measure with her on this grass.
Tell her we have measured many miles to tread a measure (dance) with her on this grass.
They say that they have measured many a mile / To tread a measure with you on this grass.
They say they have measured many miles to tread a measure with you on this grass.
It is not so. Ask them how many inches / Is in one mile? If they have measured many, / The measure then of one is easily told.
That's not true. Ask them how many inches there are in one mile. If they've measured many, they can easily tell the measure of one.
If to come hither you have measured miles, / And many miles, the Princess bids you tell / How many inches doth fill up one mile.
If you have measured miles to come here, and many miles, the Princess asks you to say how many inches make up one mile.
Tell her we measure them by weary steps.
Tell her we measure them in weary steps.
How many weary steps / Of many weary miles you have o'ergone / Are numbered in the travel of one mile?
How many weary steps of the many weary miles you've travelled are counted in the journey of one mile?

We number nothing that we spend for you. / Our duty is so rich, so infinite, / That we may do it still without account. / Vouchsafe to show the sunshine of your face, / That we, like savages, may worship it.
We count nothing we spend for you. Our devotion is so rich, so infinite, that we can always give it without counting. Please show us the sunshine of your face, so that we can worship it like savages.
My face is but a moon, and clouded too.
My face is only a moon, and a clouded one at that.
Blessed are clouds, to do as such clouds do! / Vouchsafe, bright moon, and these thy stars, to shine, / Those clouds removed, upon our watery eyne.
Blessed are the clouds that do what those clouds do! Bright moon, you and your stars, please remove those clouds and shine on our watering eyes.
O vain petitioner! Beg a greater matter! / Thou now requests but moonshine in the water.
Oh, foolish petitioner! Ask for something bigger! What you're asking for now is just moonshine in the water.
Then in our measure do but vouchsafe one change. / Thou bidd'st me beg; this begging is not strange.
Then grant us just one turn in our dance. You told me to beg; this begging isn't strange.
Play, music, then! Nay, you must do it soon.
Play, music, then! No, you must do it quickly.
Not yet? No dance! Thus change I like the moon.
Not yet? No dance! I change like the moon.
Will you not dance? How come you thus estranged?
Won't you dance? Why have you become so distant?
You took the moon at full, but now she's changed.
You caught the moon when it was full, but now it's changed.
Yet still she is the moon, and I the man. / The music plays, vouchsafe some motion to it.
But it's still the moon, and I'm the man in it. The music's playing; please move a little to it.
But your legs should do it.
Since you are strangers and come here by chance, / We'll not be nice. Take hands. We will not dance.
Since you're strangers and have come here by chance, we won't be fussy. Take hands. We won't dance.
Only to part friends. / Curtsy, sweet hearts, and so the measure ends.
Only to part as friends. Curtsy, sweethearts, and so the dance ends.
More measure of this measure! Be not nice.
More of this measure! Don't be coy.
We can afford no more at such a price.
We can't give any more at such a price.
Price you yourselves? What buys your company?
You set a price on yourselves? What would buy your company?
Then cannot we be bought. And so adieu— / Twice to your visor, and half once to you!
Then we can't be bought. And so goodbye: twice to your mask, and half a goodbye to you!
If you deny to dance, let's hold more chat.
If you refuse to dance, let's talk some more.
I am best pleased with that.
White-handed mistress, one sweet word with thee.
White-handed mistress, one sweet word with you.
Honey, and milk, and sugar: there is three.
Honey, milk and sugar: there's three.
Nay, then, two treys, an if you grow so nice, / Metheglin, wort, and malmsey. Well run, dice! / There's half a dozen sweets.
Well then, two threes, since you're so clever: mead, malt and malmsey wine. Good throw, dice! There's half a dozen sweets.
Seventh sweet, adieu. / Since you can cog, I'll play no more with you.
Seventh sweet, goodbye. Since you cheat at dice, I won't play with you any more.
Will you vouchsafe with me to change a word?
Will you be so kind as to exchange a word with me?
Say you so? Fair lord! / Take that for your "fair lady".
Is that so? Fair lord! Take that in return for your 'fair lady'.
Please it you, / As much in private, and I'll bid adieu.
If you please, as much again in private, and then I'll say goodbye.
What, was your visor made without a tongue?
What, was your mask made without a tongue?
I know the reason, lady, why you ask.
I know why you ask, lady.
O, for your reason! Quickly, sir, I long.
Oh, let's have your reason! Quickly, sir, I'm longing to hear.
You have a double tongue within your mask, / And would afford my speechless visor half.
You have two tongues inside your mask, and would like to give half to my speechless mask.
"Veal", quoth the Dutchman. Is not veal a calf?
'Veal', as the Dutchman says (meaning 'well', and 'veil'). Isn't veal a calf?
No, I'll not be your half. / Take all and wean it; it may prove an ox.
No, I won't be your other half. Take it all and wean it; it may grow into an ox.
Look how you butt yourself in these sharp mocks. / Will you give horns, chaste lady? Do not so.
Look how you butt yourself with these sharp jokes. Will you give your husband horns, chaste lady? Don't.
Then die a calf before your horns do grow.
Then die a calf before your horns grow.
One word in private with you ere I die.
One word in private with you before I die.
Bleat softly, then; the butcher hears you cry.
Bleat quietly, then; the butcher can hear you crying.

The tongues of mocking wenches are as keen / As is the razor's edge invisible, / Cutting a smaller hair than may be seen; / Above the sense of sense, so sensible / Seemeth their conference. Their conceits have wings / Fleeter than arrows, bullets, wind, thought, swifter things.

The tongues of mocking girls are as sharp as the edge of a razor too fine to see, cutting a hair smaller than can be seen. Their talk seems so subtle it is beyond the reach of the senses. Their ideas have wings swifter than arrows, bullets, wind, thought, or anything swifter.
Not one word more, my maids; break off, break off.
Not one word more, my girls; break off, break off.
By heaven, all dry-beaten with pure scoff!
By heaven, thoroughly beaten with nothing but scorn!
Farewell, mad wenches. You have simple wits.
Farewell, mad girls. You have simple wits.
Twenty adieus, my frozen Muscovites. / Are these the breed of wits so wondered at?
Twenty goodbyes, my frozen Muscovites. Are these the kind of wits people marvel at?
Tapers they are, with your sweet breaths puffed out.
They're candles, puffed out by your sweet breath.
Well-liking wits they have; gross, gross; fat, fat.
They have well-fed wits: gross, gross; fat, fat.
O poverty in wit, kingly-poor flout! / Will they not, think you, hang themselves tonight? / Or ever but in vizors show their faces? / This pert Berowne was out of countenance quite.
Oh, poverty of wit, a king's poor joke! Don't you think they'll hang themselves tonight? Or never show their faces again except in masks? This cocky Berowne was completely put out of countenance.
They were all in lamentable cases. / The King was weeping-ripe for a good word.
They were all in a pitiful state. The King was ready to cry for one kind word.
Berowne did swear himself out of all suit.
Berowne swore so much he was out of the game altogether.
Dumaine was at my service, and his sword. / "Non point," quoth I; my servant straight was mute.
Dumaine offered me his service and his sword. 'Not at all,' I said, and my servant went silent straight away.
Lord Longaville said I came o'er his heart; / And trow you what he called me?
Lord Longaville said I had come over his heart; and do you know what he called me?
Well, better wits have worn plain statute-caps. / But will you hear? The King is my love sworn.
Well, better wits have worn plain woollen caps (as citizens did). But listen: the King has sworn to be my love.
And quick Berowne hath plighted faith to me.
And quick Berowne has pledged his faith to me.
And Longaville was for my service born.
And Longaville was born to serve me.
Dumaine is mine as sure as bark on tree.
Dumaine is mine, as sure as bark is on a tree.
Madam, and pretty mistresses, give ear. / Immediately they will again be here / In their own shapes, for it can never be / They will digest this harsh indignity.
Madam, and pretty mistresses, listen. They'll be back here at once as themselves, because they'll never be able to swallow this harsh humiliation.
They will, they will, God knows, / And leap for joy, though they are lame with blows. / Therefore, change favours and, when they repair, / Blow like sweet roses in this summer air.
They will, they will, God knows, and jump for joy, though they're lame from beatings. So swap your presents back, and when they come, bloom like sweet roses in this summer air.
How "blow"? How "blow"? Speak to be understood.
What do you mean, 'bloom'? Speak so you can be understood.
Fair ladies masked are roses in their bud. / Dismasked, their damask sweet commixture shown, / Are angels vailing clouds, or roses blown.
Fair ladies in masks are roses in the bud. Unmasked, showing their sweet mixture of red and white, they are angels coming out from behind clouds, or roses in full bloom.
Avaunt, perplexity! What shall we do / If they return in their own shapes to woo?
Enough riddles! What shall we do if they come back as themselves to woo?

Good madam, if by me you'll be advised, / Let's mock them still, as well known as disguised. / Let us complain to them what fools were here, / Disguised like Muscovites in shapeless gear; / And wonder what they were, and to what end / Their shallow shows and prologue vilely penned, / And their rough carriage so ridiculous, / Should be presented at our tent to us.

Good madam, if you'll take my advice, let's keep mocking them, as much when we know them as when they were disguised. Let's complain to them about what fools were here, disguised as Muscovites in shapeless clothes, and wonder who they were, and why their shallow show, their badly written prologue and their rough, ridiculous behaviour should be put on at our tent for us.
Ladies, withdraw. The gallants are at hand.
Ladies, go inside. The gallants are close by.
Whip to our tents, as roes run o'er the land.
Dash to our tents, as deer run across the land.
Fair sir, God save you. Where's the Princess?
Good sir, God save you. Where is the Princess?
Gone to her tent. Please it your Majesty / Command me any service to her thither?
Gone to her tent. Would Your Majesty like me to take any message to her there?
That she vouchsafe me audience for one word.
That she will grant me a hearing for one word.
I will; and so will she, I know, my lord.
I will; and so will she, I know, my lord.

This fellow pecks up wit as pigeons peas / And utters it again when God doth please. / He is wit's pedlar, and retails his wares / At wakes and wassails, meetings, markets, fairs; / And we that sell by gross, the Lord doth know, / Have not the grace to grace it with such show. / This gallant pins the wenches on his sleeve. / Had he been Adam, he had tempted Eve. / He can carve too, and lisp. Why, this is he / That kissed his hand away in courtesy. / This is the ape of form, Monsieur the Nice, / That, when he plays at tables, chides the dice / In honourable terms. Nay, he can sing / A mean most meanly; and in ushering / Mend him who can. The ladies call him sweet. / The stairs, as he treads on them, kiss his feet. / This is the flower that smiles on everyone, / To show his teeth as white as whale's bone; / And consciences that will not die in debt / Pay him the due of "honey-tongued Boyet".

This fellow pecks up wit the way pigeons peck up peas, and spits it out again whenever God pleases. He's a pedlar of wit, and sells his goods retail at festivals and parties, meetings, markets and fairs; and we who sell wholesale, the Lord knows, haven't the grace to show it off like that. This gallant has the girls pinned to his sleeve. If he'd been Adam, he'd have tempted Eve. He can carve at table, too, and lisp. Why, this is the man who kissed his hand away being polite. This is the ape of good manners, Monsieur Fastidious, who, when he plays backgammon, scolds the dice in respectful language. Why, he can sing a middle part most moderately; and as a gentleman usher, let anyone beat him if they can. The ladies call him sweet. The stairs kiss his feet as he walks on them. This is the flower that smiles at everyone, to show his teeth as white as whalebone; and people who don't want to die in debt pay him his due by calling him 'honey-tongued Boyet'.
A blister on his sweet tongue, with my heart, / That put Armado's page out of his part!
A blister on his sweet tongue, with all my heart, for putting Armado's page off his lines!
See where it comes! Behaviour, what wert thou / Till this man showed thee, and what art thou now?
Look, here he comes! Good manners, what were you before this man displayed you, and what are you now?
All hail, sweet madam, and fair time of day.
All hail, sweet madam, and good day to you.
"Fair" in "all hail" is foul, as I conceive.
'Fair' and 'hail' don't go together, as I see it (hail is foul weather).
Construe my speeches better, if you may.
Interpret my words better, if you can.
Then wish me better. I will give you leave.
Then wish me better. I'll allow you to.
We came to visit you, and purpose now / To lead you to our court. Vouchsafe it then.
We came to visit you, and we mean now to take you to our court. Please agree to it.
This field shall hold me, and so hold your vow. / Nor God nor I delights in perjured men.
This field will hold me, and so you can hold to your vow. Neither God nor I takes pleasure in men who break their oaths.
Rebuke me not for that which you provoke. / The virtue of your eye must break my oath.
Don't scold me for what you cause. The power of your eyes must break my oath.

You nickname virtue: "vice" you should have spoke; / For virtue's office never breaks men's troth. / Now by my maiden honour, yet as pure / As the unsullied lily, I protest, / A world of torments though I should endure, / I would not yield to be your house's guest, / So much I hate a breaking cause to be / Of heavenly oaths, vowed with integrity.

You call it by the wrong name: you should have said 'vice', not 'virtue', because virtue never makes men break their word. Now, by my maiden honour, which is still as pure as the spotless lily, I swear that even if I had to suffer a world of torments I would not agree to be a guest in your house; I so hate to be the cause of breaking holy oaths, sworn in good faith.
O, you have lived in desolation here, / Unseen, unvisited, much to our shame.
Oh, you've lived out here in loneliness, unseen and unvisited, much to our shame.
Not so, my lord. It is not so, I swear. / We have had pastimes here and pleasant game. / A mess of Russians left us but of late.
Not so, my lord. It isn't so, I swear. We've had amusements here and pleasant games. A group of Russians left us only recently.
Ay, in truth, my lord. / Trim gallants, full of courtship and of state.
Yes, truly, my lord. Smart gallants, full of courtly manners and dignity.

Madam, speak true. It is not so, my lord. / My lady, to the manner of the days, / In courtesy gives undeserving praise. / We four indeed confronted were with four / In Russian habit. Here they stayed an hour / And talked apace; and in that hour, my lord, / They did not bless us with one happy word. / I dare not call them fools; but this I think, / When they are thirsty, fools would fain have drink.

Madam, tell the truth. It isn't so, my lord. My lady, following the fashion of the times, politely gives undeserved praise. We four were indeed confronted by four men in Russian dress. They stayed here an hour and talked a lot; and in that hour, my lord, they didn't bless us with one good word. I daren't call them fools; but this I do think: when they're thirsty, fools would like a drink.

This jest is dry to me. My gentle sweet, / Your wit makes wise things foolish. When we greet, / With eyes' best seeing, heaven's fiery eye, / By light we lose light. Your capacity / Is of that nature that to your huge store / Wise things seem foolish and rich things but poor.

This joke seems dry to me. My gentle sweet, your wit makes wise things look foolish. When we stare at the sun, heaven's fiery eye, with our best eyesight, we lose our sight through too much light. Your mind is such that, beside its huge store, wise things look foolish and rich things look poor.
This proves you wise and rich, for in my eye—
That proves you are wise and rich, because in my eyes...
I am a fool, and full of poverty.
I am a fool, and full of poverty.
But that you take what doth to you belong, / It were a fault to snatch words from my tongue.
If you weren't taking what belongs to you, it would be wrong to snatch words out of my mouth.
O, I am yours, and all that I possess.
Oh, I am yours, and everything I own.
Which of the visors was it that you wore?
Which of the masks was it you wore?
Where, when, what visor? Why demand you this?
Where, when, what mask? Why do you ask that?
There, then, that visor; that superfluous case / That hid the worse and showed the better face.
There, then, that mask; that unnecessary cover that hid the worse face and showed the better one.
We are descried. They'll mock us now downright.
We've been found out. They'll mock us openly now.
Let us confess and turn it to a jest.
Let's confess and turn it into a joke.
Amazed, my lord? Why looks your Highness sad?
Bewildered, my lord? Why does Your Highness look sad?
Help! Hold his brows! He'll swoon. Why look you pale? / Seasick, I think, coming from Muscovy.
Help! Hold his head! He'll faint. Why do you look pale? Seasick, I think, from the voyage from Muscovy.

Thus pour the stars down plagues for perjury. / Can any face of brass hold longer out? / Here stand I, lady; dart thy skill at me. / Bruise me with scorn, confound me with a flout, / Thrust thy sharp wit quite through my ignorance, / Cut me to pieces with thy keen conceit, / And I will wish thee never more to dance, / Nor never more in Russian habit wait. / O, never will I trust to speeches penned, / Nor to the motion of a school-boy's tongue, / Nor never come in visor to my friend, / Nor woo in rhyme like a blind harper's song. / Taffeta phrases, silken terms precise, / Three-piled hyperboles, spruce affectation, / Figures pedantical: these summer flies / Have blown me full of maggot ostentation. / I do forswear them, and I here protest, / By this white glove—how white the hand, God knows!— / Henceforth my wooing mind shall be expressed / In russet yeas and honest kersey noes. / And, to begin: wench, so God help me, law, / My love to thee is sound, sans crack or flaw.

This is how the stars rain down plagues for breaking oaths. Can any brazen face hold out any longer? Here I stand, lady; throw your skill at me. Bruise me with scorn, crush me with a jeer, thrust your sharp wit right through my ignorance, cut me to pieces with your keen ideas, and I'll never ask you to dance again, or wait on you in Russian dress again. Oh, I'll never again trust prepared speeches, or a schoolboy's tongue reciting them, or come in a mask to my love, or woo in rhyme like a blind harper's song. Silky phrases, precise, elegant terms, velvet-thick exaggerations, spruce affectation, pedantic figures of speech: these summer flies have filled me with the maggots of showing off. I renounce them, and I swear here, by this white glove (how white the hand is, God knows!), that from now on my wooing will be expressed in plain homespun yeses and honest woollen noes. And to begin: girl, so help me God, la, my love for you is sound, sans crack or flaw.

Yet I have a trick / Of the old rage. Bear with me, I am sick; / I'll leave it by degrees. Soft, let us see: / Write "Lord have mercy on us" on those three. / They are infected; in their hearts it lies; / They have the plague, and caught it of your eyes. / These lords are visited. You are not free, / For the Lord's tokens on you do I see.

I still have a touch of the old disease. Be patient with me, I'm sick; I'll give it up gradually. Wait, let's see. Write 'Lord have mercy on us' on those three (as on plague houses). They are infected; it's in their hearts. They have the plague, and caught it from your eyes. These lords are stricken. And you're not free of it, because I can see the Lord's tokens (the plague spots, and their love-gifts) on you.
No, they are free that gave these tokens to us.
No, the ones who gave us these tokens are free.
Our states are forfeit. Seek not to undo us.
Our estates are forfeit. Don't try to ruin us.
It is not so. For how can this be true, / That you stand forfeit, being those that sue?
That's not so. How can it be true that you're forfeit, when you are the ones bringing the lawsuit?
Peace! for I will not have to do with you.
Quiet! I won't have anything to do with you.
Nor shall not, if I do as I intend.
And you won't, if I do what I intend.
Speak for yourselves. My wit is at an end.
Speak for yourselves. My wit has run out.
Teach us, sweet madam, for our rude transgression / Some fair excuse.
Teach us, sweet madam, some good excuse for our rude offence.
The fairest is confession. / Were not you here but even now, disguised?
The best is confession. Weren't you here just now, in disguise?
And did you know what you were doing?
When you then were here, / What did you whisper in your lady's ear?
When you were here, then, what did you whisper in your lady's ear?
That more than all the world I did respect her.
That I respected her more than all the world.
When she shall challenge this, you will reject her.
When she holds you to that, you'll reject her.
Peace, peace, forbear! / Your oath once broke, you force not to forswear.
Quiet, quiet, stop! Once you've broken one oath, you don't mind breaking another.
Despise me when I break this oath of mine.
Despise me if I break this oath of mine.
I will; and therefore keep it. Rosaline, / What did the Russian whisper in your ear?
I will; so keep it. Rosaline, what did the Russian whisper in your ear?
Madam, he swore that he did hold me dear / As precious eyesight, and did value me / Above this world; adding thereto, moreover, / That he would wed me, or else die my lover.
Madam, he swore that he held me as dear as his precious eyesight and valued me above the whole world; and he added, besides, that he would marry me or else die loving me.
God give thee joy of him! The noble lord / Most honourably doth uphold his word.
God give you joy of him! The noble lord keeps his word most honourably.
What mean you, madam? By my life, my troth, / I never swore this lady such an oath.
What do you mean, madam? By my life and my faith, I never swore such an oath to this lady.
By heaven, you did! And to confirm it plain, / You gave me this. But take it, sir, again.
By heaven, you did! And to prove it clearly, you gave me this. But take it back, sir.
My faith and this the Princess I did give. / I knew her by this jewel on her sleeve.
I gave my promise and this to the Princess. I recognised her by this jewel on her sleeve.
Pardon me, sir, this jewel did she wear, / And Lord Berowne, I thank him, is my dear. / What, will you have me, or your pearl again?
Excuse me, sir, she was wearing this jewel; and Lord Berowne, I thank him, is my darling. What, will you have me, or your pearl back?

Neither of either; I remit both twain. / I see the trick on't. Here was a consent, / Knowing aforehand of our merriment, / To dash it like a Christmas comedy. / Some carry-tale, some please-man, some slight zany, / Some mumble-news, some trencher-knight, some Dick, / That smiles his cheek in years and knows the trick / To make my lady laugh when she's disposed, / Told our intents before; which once disclosed, / The ladies did change favours, and then we, / Following the signs, wooed but the sign of she. / Now, to our perjury to add more terror, / We are again forsworn in will and error. / Much upon this 'tis. [To Boyet] And might not you / Forestall our sport, to make us thus untrue? / Do not you know my lady's foot by th' squier, / And laugh upon the apple of her eye? / And stand between her back, sir, and the fire, / Holding a trencher, jesting merrily? / You put our page out. Go, you are allowed; / Die when you will, a smock shall be your shroud. / You leer upon me, do you? There's an eye / Wounds like a leaden sword.

Neither one nor the other; I give up both. I see the trick of it. There was a plot here: knowing about our fun beforehand, they set out to spoil it like a Christmas comedy. Some tell-tale, some flatterer, some lowly clown, some gossip, some hanger-on at the dinner table, some fellow who smiles his face into wrinkles and knows the trick of making my lady laugh when she's in the mood, told them our plans in advance. Once that was out, the ladies swapped favours, and we, following the signs, wooed only the sign of our lady. Now, to add more terror to our perjury, we've broken our oaths again, in intention and by mistake. That's about it. [To Boyet] And wasn't it you who spoiled our fun ahead of time, making us false like this? Don't you know my lady's foot by the ruler, and laugh in the apple of her eye, and stand between her back and the fire holding a plate, joking merrily? You put our page off his lines. Go on, you're the licensed fool; die when you like, a woman's slip will be your shroud. You leer at me, do you? There's an eye that wounds like a lead sword.
Full merrily / Hath this brave manage, this career, been run.
Very merrily this fine gallop, this charge, has been run.
Lo, he is tilting straight! Peace! I have done.
Look, he's charging straight at me with his lance! Quiet! I've finished.
Welcome, pure wit! Thou part'st a fair fray.
Welcome, pure wit! You've broken up a good fight.
O Lord, sir, they would know / Whether the three Worthies shall come in or no.
Oh Lord, sir, they want to know whether the three Worthies should come in or not.
No, sir; but it is vara fine, / For every one pursents three.
No, sir; but it's very fine, because each one presents three.
And three times thrice is nine.
And three times three is nine.
Not so, sir, under correction, sir, I hope it is not so. / You cannot beg us, sir, I can assure you, sir; we know what we know. / I hope, sir, three times thrice, sir—
Not so, sir, if you'll allow me to correct you, sir; I hope it isn't so. You can't make fools of us, sir, I assure you, sir; we know what we know. I hope, sir, three times three, sir...
Under correction, sir, we know whereuntil it doth amount.
With respect, sir, we know what it comes to.
By Jove, I always took three threes for nine.
By Jove, I always thought three threes made nine.
O Lord, sir, it were pity you should get your living by reckoning, sir.
Oh Lord, sir, it would be a pity if you had to earn your living by arithmetic, sir.
O Lord, sir, the parties themselves, the actors, sir, will show / whereuntil it doth amount. For mine own part, I am, as they say, but to / parfect one man in one poor man—Pompion the Great, sir.
Oh Lord, sir, the parties themselves, the actors, sir, will show what it comes to. For my own part, I am, as they say, only to perform one man in one poor man: Pompion (pumpkin) the Great, sir.
Art thou one of the Worthies?
Are you one of the Worthies?
It pleased them to think me worthy of Pompey the Great. For mine own / part, I know not the degree of the Worthy, but I am to stand for him.
They were good enough to think me worthy of Pompey the Great. For my own part, I don't know how high up the Worthy is, but I'm to stand in for him.
Go and tell them to get ready.
We will turn it finely off, sir; we will take some care.
We'll carry it off nicely, sir; we'll take some care.
Berowne, they will shame us. Let them not approach.
Berowne, they'll shame us. Don't let them come.
We are shame-proof, my lord, and 'tis some policy / To have one show worse than the King's and his company.
We're shame-proof, my lord; and it's good policy to have one show that's worse than the King's and his company's.
I say they shall not come.

Nay, my good lord, let me o'errule you now. / That sport best pleases that doth least know how, / Where zeal strives to content, and the contents / Die in the zeal of that which it presents; / Their form confounded makes most form in mirth, / When great things labouring perish in their birth.

No, my good lord, let me overrule you now. The entertainment that pleases most is the one that knows least how to do it: where eagerness tries to please, and the content dies in the eagerness of those presenting it. Their efforts going wrong makes the best kind of fun, when great things, struggling to be born, die in the attempt.
A right description of our sport, my lord.
An exact description of our own entertainment, my lord.
Anointed, I implore so much expense of thy royal sweet breath as will / utter a brace of words.
Anointed one, I beg as much of your royal sweet breath as will speak a couple of words.
He speaks not like a man of God his making.
He doesn't speak like a man God made.

That is all one, my fair, sweet, honey monarch; for, I protest, the / schoolmaster is exceeding fantastical; too, too vain, too, too vain. / But we will put it, as they say, to fortuna de la guerra. I wish you / the peace of mind, most royal couplement!

It's all the same, my fair, sweet, honey monarch; for, I declare, the schoolmaster is extremely fantastical; too, too vain, too, too vain. But we'll leave it, as they say, to 'fortuna de la guerra', the fortune of war. I wish you peace of mind, most royal couple!

Here is like to be a good presence of Worthies. He presents Hector of / Troy; the swain, Pompey the Great; the parish curate, Alexander; / Armado's page, Hercules; the pedant, Judas Maccabaeus. / And if these four Worthies in their first show thrive, / These four will change habits and present the other five.

It looks like there'll be a good array of Worthies. He plays Hector of Troy; the peasant, Pompey the Great; the parish curate, Alexander; Armado's page, Hercules; the schoolmaster, Judas Maccabaeus. And if these four Worthies do well in their first show, these four will change costumes and present the other five.
There is five in the first show.
There are five in the first show.
The pedant, the braggart, the hedge-priest, the fool, and the boy. / Abate throw at novum, and the whole world again / Cannot pick out five such, take each one in his vein.
The schoolmaster, the braggart, the hedge-priest, the fool and the boy. Except for a lucky throw at dice, the whole world couldn't pick out another five like them, each in his own way.
The ship is under sail, and here she comes amain.
The ship is under sail, and here she comes at full speed.
You lie, you are not he.
with a leopard's head on his knee (as on a coat of arms).
Well said, old mocker. I must needs be friends with thee.
Well said, old mocker. I'll have to be friends with you.
I Pompey am, Pompey surnamed the Big.
I Pompey am, Pompey surnamed the Big...

It is "Great", sir; Pompey surnamed the Great, / That oft in field, with targe and shield, did make my foe to sweat. / And travelling along this coast, I here am come by chance, / And lay my arms before the legs of this sweet lass of France. / If your ladyship would say, "Thanks, Pompey", I had done.

It is 'Great', sir. 'Pompey surnamed the Great, who often in the field, with shield and buckler, made my enemy sweat; and travelling along this coast, I have come here by chance, and lay my arms before the legs of this sweet lass of France.' If your ladyship would say 'Thanks, Pompey', I'd be done.
'Tis not so much worth; but I hope I was perfect. I made a little fault / in "Great".
It isn't worth that much; but I hope I was word-perfect. I made a little mistake on 'Great'.
My hat to a halfpenny, Pompey proves the best Worthy.
I'll bet my hat against a halfpenny that Pompey turns out the best Worthy.
When in the world I lived, I was the world's commander; / By east, west, north, and south, I spread my conquering might. / My scutcheon plain declares that I am Alisander.
'When I lived in the world, I was the world's commander; east, west, north and south, I spread my conquering might. My coat of arms plainly declares that I am Alisander.'
Your nose says, no, you are not; for it stands to right.
Your nose says no, you are not, because it stands too straight (Alexander's head was said to tilt).
Your nose smells "no" in this, most tender-smelling knight.
Your nose smells 'no' in this, most delicate-smelling knight (Alexander's body was said to smell sweet).
The conqueror is dismayed. Proceed, good Alexander.
The conqueror is upset. Carry on, good Alexander.
When in the world I lived, I was the world's commander—
'When I lived in the world, I was the world's commander...'
Most true; 'tis right. You were so, Alisander.
Very true; that's right. You were, Alisander.
Take away the conqueror, take away Alisander.
Take away the conqueror, take away Alisander.

[To Sir Nathaniel] O sir, you have overthrown Alisander the / Conqueror. You will be scraped out of the painted cloth for this. Your / lion, that holds his pole-axe sitting on a close-stool, will be given / to Ajax. He will be the ninth Worthy. A conqueror, and afeard to speak? / Run away for shame, Alisander. [Nathaniel retires] There, an't shall / please you, a foolish mild man; an honest man, look you, and soon / dashed. He is a marvellous good neighbour, faith, and a very good / bowler; but for Alisander, alas you see how 'tis—a little o'erparted. / But there are Worthies a-coming will speak their mind in some other / sort.

[To Sir Nathaniel] Oh, sir, you've overthrown Alisander the Conqueror! You'll be scraped off the painted wall-hanging for this. Your lion holding his battle-axe sitting on a toilet will be given to Ajax: he'll be the ninth Worthy. A conqueror, and afraid to speak? Run away for shame, Alisander. [Nathaniel retires] There, if you please, a foolish, mild man; an honest man, you see, and easily flustered. He's a marvellously good neighbour, honestly, and a very good bowler; but as for Alisander, alas, you see how it is: a little out of his depth. But there are Worthies coming who'll speak their minds in a different way.

Great Hercules is presented by this imp, / Whose club killed Cerberus, that three-headed canus, / And when he was a babe, a child, a shrimp, / Thus did he strangle serpents in his manus. / Quoniam he seemeth in minority, / Ergo I come with this apology. / Keep some state in thy exit, and vanish.

'Great Hercules is played by this imp, whose club killed Cerberus, that three-headed "canus" (dog); and when he was a baby, a child, a shrimp, he strangled serpents like this in his "manus" (hands). "Quoniam", since, he seems to be under age, "ergo", therefore, I come with this explanation.' Make a dignified exit, and vanish.
Not Iscariot, sir. / Judas I am, ycleped Maccabaeus.
Not Iscariot, sir. 'Judas I am, called Maccabaeus.'
Judas Maccabaeus clipped is plain Judas.
Judas Maccabaeus cut short is plain Judas.
A kissing traitor. How art thou proved Judas?
A kissing traitor. How do you prove you're Judas?
The more shame for you, Judas.
All the more shame on you, Judas.
Begin, sir; you are my elder.
You begin, sir; you are my elder.
Well followed. Judas was hanged on an elder.
Well followed up: Judas was hanged on an elder tree.
I will not be put out of countenance.
I won't be put out of countenance (made to lose my nerve).
The carved head on a lute.
A death's face in a ring.
A skull on a memorial ring.
The face of an old Roman coin, scarce seen.
The face of an old Roman coin, worn almost away.
The knob on the handle of Caesar's sword.
The carved-bone face on a flask.
The carved bone face on a powder flask.
Saint George's half-cheek in a brooch.
Saint George's profile on a brooch.
Ay, and in a brooch of lead.
Yes, and a lead brooch at that.
Ay, and worn in the cap of a tooth-drawer. / And now forward, for we have put thee in countenance.
Yes, and worn in the hat of a tooth-puller. And now go on, for we've given you some faces.
You have put me out of countenance.
You've put me out of countenance.
False. We have given thee faces.
Not true. We've given you lots of faces.
But you have outfaced them all.
An thou wert a lion, we would do so.
If you were a lion, we'd do just that.
Therefore, as he is an ass, let him go. / And so adieu, sweet Jude. Nay, why dost thou stay?
So, since he's an ass, let him go. And so goodbye, sweet Jude. Well, why are you still here?
For the latter end of his name.
For the end of his name.
For the ass to the Jude? Give it him. Jud-as, away!
For the 'ass' to go after 'Jude'? Give it to him. Jud-as, away!
This is not generous, not gentle, not humble.
This isn't generous, not gentlemanly, not humble.
A light for Monsieur Judas! It grows dark; he may stumble.
A light for Monsieur Judas! It's getting dark; he may stumble. (Judas carried a lantern when he betrayed Christ.)
Alas, poor Maccabaeus, how hath he been baited!
Alas, poor Maccabaeus, how he's been baited!
Hide thy head, Achilles. Here comes Hector in arms.
Hide your head, Achilles. Here comes Hector in armour.
Though my mocks come home by me, I will now be merry.
Even if my jokes come back to bite me, I'll be merry now.
Hector was but a Trojan in respect of this.
Hector was only a Trojan (a fine fellow) compared with this.
I think Hector was not so clean-timbered.
I don't think Hector was so well built.
His leg is too big for Hector's.
His leg is too big for Hector's.
No, he is best endued in the small.
No, he's best equipped in the slender part (the lower leg).
He's a god or a painter, for he makes faces.
He's a god or a painter, because he makes faces.
The armipotent Mars, of lances the almighty, / Gave Hector a gift—
'The arm-mighty Mars, almighty in lances, gave Hector a gift...'

Peace! / The armipotent Mars, of lances the almighty, / Gave Hector a gift, the heir of Ilion; / A man so breathed that certain he would fight, yea, / From morn till night, out of his pavilion. / I am that flower—

Quiet! 'The arm-mighty Mars, almighty in lances, gave Hector a gift, the heir of Troy; a man of such stamina that he would certainly fight, yes, from morning to night, outside his tent. I am that flower...'
Sweet Lord Longaville, rein thy tongue.
Sweet Lord Longaville, rein in your tongue.
I must rather give it the rein, for it runs against Hector.
I must rather give it its head, because it's running against Hector.
Yes, and Hector's a greyhound (and will outrun it).

The sweet war-man is dead and rotten. Sweet chucks, beat not the bones / of the buried. When he breathed, he was a man. But I will forward with / my device. [To the Princess] Sweet royalty, bestow on me the sense / of hearing.

The sweet warrior is dead and rotten. Sweet chicks, don't beat the bones of the buried. When he was alive, he was a man. But I will go on with my show. [To the Princess] Sweet royalty, grant me your sense of hearing.
Speak, brave Hector; we are much delighted.
Speak, brave Hector; we are very pleased.
I do adore thy sweet Grace's slipper.
I adore your sweet Grace's slipper.
He loves her by the foot.
He may not by the yard.
He can't love her by the yard (a bawdy pun).
This Hector far surmounted Hannibal. / The party is gone—
'This Hector far surpassed Hannibal...' The party is gone...
Fellow Hector, she is gone; she is two months on her way.
Fellow Hector, she is gone; she's two months gone.
Faith, unless you play the honest Trojan, the poor wench is cast away. / She's quick; the child brags in her belly already. 'Tis yours.
Honestly, unless you play the honest Trojan, the poor girl is ruined. She's pregnant; the child is already showing off in her belly. It's yours.
Dost thou infamonize me among potentates? Thou shalt die.
Do you defame me in front of rulers? You will die.
Then shall Hector be whipped for Jaquenetta that is quick by him, and / hanged for Pompey that is dead by him.
Then Hector will be whipped for Jaquenetta, who's pregnant by him, and hanged for Pompey, who'll be dead by him.
Greater than "Great"! Great, great, great Pompey! Pompey the Huge!
Greater than 'Great'! Great, great, great Pompey! Pompey the Huge!
Pompey is moved. More Ates, more Ates! Stir them on, stir them on!
Pompey is angry. More goddesses of discord, more! Stir them up, stir them up!
Ay, if he have no more man's blood in his belly than will sup a flea.
Yes, if he hasn't more man's blood in his belly than would feed a flea.
By the north pole, I do challenge thee.
By the North Pole, I challenge you.
I will not fight with a pole, like a northern man. I'll slash, I'll do / it by the sword. I bepray you, let me borrow my arms again.
I won't fight with a pole, like a northern man. I'll slash; I'll do it with the sword. Please, let me borrow my weapons back.
Make room for the angry Worthies!
I'll do it in my shirt.
Master, let me take you a buttonhole lower. Do you not see Pompey is / uncasing for the combat? What mean you? You will lose your reputation.
Master, let me take you down a peg. Don't you see Pompey is stripping for the fight? What do you mean by it? You'll lose your reputation.
Gentlemen and soldiers, pardon me. I will not combat in my shirt.
Gentlemen and soldiers, forgive me. I will not fight in my shirt.
You may not deny it. Pompey hath made the challenge.
You can't refuse. Pompey has made the challenge.
Sweet bloods, I both may and will.
Sweet fellows, I both can and will.
The naked truth of it is, I have no shirt. I go woolward for penance.
The naked truth is, I have no shirt. I wear wool next to my skin as a penance.
True, and it was enjoined him in Rome for want of linen; since when, / I'll be sworn, he wore none but a dishclout of Jaquenetta's, and that / he wears next his heart for a favour.

True, and it was ordered as a penance for him in Rome for lack of linen; since then, I'll swear, he's worn nothing but one of Jaquenetta's dishcloths, and he wears that next to his heart as a love-token.
Welcome, Marcadé, / But that thou interruptest our merriment.
Welcome, Marcadé, except that you interrupt our fun.
I am sorry, madam, for the news I bring / Is heavy in my tongue. The King your father—
I'm sorry, madam, because the news I bring is heavy on my tongue. The King your father...
Even so. My tale is told.
It is so. My message is delivered.
Worthies away! The scene begins to cloud.
Worthies, away! The scene is clouding over.
For mine own part, I breathe free breath. I have seen the day of wrong / through the little hole of discretion, and I will right myself like a / soldier.
For my own part, I breathe freely. I have seen how I was wronged through the little hole of discretion, and I will right myself like a soldier.
Boyet, prepare. I will away tonight.
Boyet, get ready. I will leave tonight.
Madam, not so. I do beseech you stay.
Madam, don't. I beg you to stay.

Prepare, I say. I thank you, gracious lords, / For all your fair endeavours, and entreat, / Out of a new-sad soul, that you vouchsafe / In your rich wisdom to excuse or hide / The liberal opposition of our spirits, / If over-boldly we have borne ourselves / In the converse of breath; your gentleness / Was guilty of it. Farewell, worthy lord! / A heavy heart bears not a nimble tongue. / Excuse me so, coming too short of thanks / For my great suit so easily obtained.

Get ready, I say. I thank you, gracious lords, for all your kind efforts, and I ask, from a newly saddened soul, that in your rich wisdom you forgive or overlook the free way our spirits have opposed yours, if we have behaved too boldly in our talk; your kindness was to blame for it. Farewell, worthy lord! A heavy heart doesn't have a nimble tongue. Please excuse me, then, for falling short in thanking you for my great request, so easily granted.

The extreme parts of time extremely forms / All causes to the purpose of his speed, / And often at his very loose decides / That which long process could not arbitrate. / And though the mourning brow of progeny / Forbid the smiling courtesy of love / The holy suit which fain it would convince, / Yet, since love's argument was first on foot, / Let not the cloud of sorrow jostle it / From what it purposed; since to wail friends lost / Is not by much so wholesome-profitable / As to rejoice at friends but newly found.

The last moments of time often shape every matter to fit its haste, and at the very last moment decide what a long process couldn't settle. And though a daughter's mourning face forbids love's smiling courtesy to press the holy suit it would like to win, still, since love's case was started first, don't let the cloud of sorrow push it aside from what it intended; for mourning lost friends is not nearly as healthy or profitable as rejoicing at friends just found.
I understand you not. My griefs are double.
I don't understand you. My griefs are doubled.

Honest plain words best pierce the ear of grief; / And by these badges understand the King. / For your fair sakes have we neglected time, / Played foul play with our oaths. Your beauty, ladies, / Hath much deformed us, fashioning our humours / Even to the opposed end of our intents; / And what in us hath seemed ridiculous— / As love is full of unbefitting strains, / All wanton as a child, skipping and vain, / Formed by the eye and therefore, like the eye, / Full of strange shapes, of habits and of forms, / Varying in subjects as the eye doth roll / To every varied object in his glance; / Which parti-coated presence of loose love / Put on by us, if, in your heavenly eyes, / Have misbecomed our oaths and gravities, / Those heavenly eyes that look into these faults / Suggested us to make. Therefore, ladies, / Our love being yours, the error that love makes / Is likewise yours. We to ourselves prove false / By being once false for ever to be true / To those that make us both—fair ladies, you. / And even that falsehood, in itself a sin, / Thus purifies itself and turns to grace.

Honest plain words reach the ear of grief best, and these will help you understand the King. For your lovely sakes we've wasted our time and played false with our oaths. Your beauty, ladies, has changed us greatly, shaping our moods to the very opposite of what we intended. And whatever in us has seemed ridiculous (for love is full of unsuitable impulses, as wanton as a child, skipping and foolish; it is born in the eye, and so, like the eye, it is full of strange shapes, habits and forms, changing its subject as the eye rolls to every different object it glances at): if this motley costume of free love that we put on has, in your heavenly eyes, seemed unfit for our oaths and our dignity, it was those heavenly eyes, which see these faults, that tempted us to commit them. So, ladies, since our love is yours, the mistakes love makes are yours too. We are false to ourselves by being false once, in order to be true for ever to those who make us both false and true: fair ladies, you. And even that falseness, which is a sin in itself, purifies itself in this way and turns to grace.

We have received your letters, full of love; / Your favours, the ambassadors of love; / And in our maiden council rated them / At courtship, pleasant jest, and courtesy, / As bombast and as lining to the time. / But more devout than this in our respects / Have we not been; and therefore met your loves / In their own fashion, like a merriment.

We received your letters, full of love, and your gifts, love's ambassadors; and in our girls' council we rated them as courtship, a pleasant joke and good manners, padding to fill the time. We have not taken them more seriously than that; and so we met your love in its own fashion, as a game.
Our letters, madam, showed much more than jest.
Our letters, madam, showed much more than a joke.
We did not quote them so.
We didn't read them that way.
Now, at the latest minute of the hour, / Grant us your loves.
Now, at the very last minute of the hour, grant us your love.

A time, methinks, too short / To make a world-without-end bargain in. / No, no, my lord, your Grace is perjured much, / Full of dear guiltiness; and therefore this: / If for my love—as there is no such cause— / You will do aught, this shall you do for me: / Your oath I will not trust, but go with speed / To some forlorn and naked hermitage, / Remote from all the pleasures of the world, / There stay until the twelve celestial signs / Have brought about the annual reckoning. / If this austere insociable life / Change not your offer made in heat of blood; / If frosts and fasts, hard lodging and thin weeds, / Nip not the gaudy blossoms of your love, / But that it bear this trial, and last love; / Then, at the expiration of the year, / Come challenge me, challenge me by these deserts, / And, by this virgin palm now kissing thine, / I will be thine. And, till that instance, shut / My woeful self up in a mournful house, / Raining the tears of lamentation / For the remembrance of my father's death. / If this thou do deny, let our hands part, / Neither entitled in the other's heart.

A time far too short, I think, to make an eternal bargain in. No, no, my lord, Your Grace has broken many oaths and is full of grievous guilt; so here is what I say. If you will do anything for my love (though there's no reason why you should), this is what you must do for me. I won't trust your oath; instead, go straight away to some lonely, bare hermitage, far from all the pleasures of the world, and stay there until the twelve signs of the zodiac have brought round a full year. If this harsh, solitary life doesn't change the offer you made in the heat of passion; if frosts and fasting, a hard bed and thin clothes don't nip the showy blossoms of your love; if it survives this test and stays love: then, at the end of the year, come and claim me, claim me by what you have earned, and, by this virgin hand now kissing yours, I will be yours. Until then I'll shut my sorrowful self up in a house of mourning, raining tears of grief in memory of my father's death. If you refuse this, let our hands part, and neither have any claim on the other's heart.
If this, or more than this, I would deny, / To flatter up these powers of mine with rest, / The sudden hand of death close up mine eye! / Hence hermit, then. My heart is in thy breast.
If I would refuse this, or more than this, to pamper my body with comfort, may the sudden hand of death close my eyes! Off to the hermitage, then. My heart is in your breast.
And what to me, my love? But what to me? / A wife?
And what for me, my love? But what for me? A wife?
A beard, fair health, and honesty; / With threefold love I wish you all these three.
A beard, good health and honesty; I wish you all three with three times as much love.
O, shall I say, "I thank you, gentle wife"?
Oh, shall I say, 'Thank you, gentle wife'?
No so, my lord. A twelvemonth and a day / I'll mark no words that smooth-faced wooers say. / Come when the King doth to my lady come; / Then, if I have much love, I'll give you some.
Not so, my lord. For a year and a day I'll ignore anything smooth-faced wooers say. Come when the King comes to my lady; then, if I have plenty of love, I'll give you some.
I'll serve thee true and faithfully till then.
I'll serve you truly and faithfully until then.
Yet swear not, lest ye be forsworn again.
But don't swear it, in case you break your oath again.
At the twelvemonth's end / I'll change my black gown for a faithful friend.
At the end of the year, I'll exchange my black mourning gown for a faithful friend.
I'll stay with patience, but the time is long.
I'll wait patiently; but the time is long.
The liker you; few taller are so young.
All the more like you; few men so young are so tall.
Studies my lady? Mistress, look on me. / Behold the window of my heart, mine eye, / What humble suit attends thy answer there. / Impose some service on me for thy love.
Is my lady deep in thought? Mistress, look at me. See in the window of my heart, my eye, what humble request waits there for your answer. Set me some task for your love.

Oft have I heard of you, my Lord Berowne, / Before I saw you; and the world's large tongue / Proclaims you for a man replete with mocks, / Full of comparisons and wounding flouts, / Which you on all estates will execute / That lie within the mercy of your wit. / To weed this wormwood from your fruitful brain, / And therewithal to win me, if you please, / Without the which I am not to be won, / You shall this twelvemonth term from day to day / Visit the speechless sick, and still converse / With groaning wretches; and your task shall be, / With all the fierce endeavour of your wit / To enforce the pained impotent to smile.

I'd often heard of you, my Lord Berowne, before I saw you; and the world's broad tongue proclaims you a man full of mockery, full of comparisons and wounding jeers, which you fire at people of every rank who come within range of your wit. To weed this bitter wormwood out of your fertile brain, and at the same time to win me, if you want to (and without that I can't be won), you shall spend this year, day after day, visiting the speechless sick and talking constantly with groaning wretches; and your task will be, with all the fierce effort of your wit, to force the pained and helpless to smile.
To move wild laughter in the throat of death? / It cannot be, it is impossible. / Mirth cannot move a soul in agony.
To stir wild laughter in the throat of death? It can't be done; it's impossible. Mirth can't move a soul in agony.

Why, that's the way to choke a gibing spirit, / Whose influence is begot of that loose grace / Which shallow laughing hearers give to fools. / A jest's prosperity lies in the ear / Of him that hears it, never in the tongue / Of him that makes it. Then, if sickly ears, / Deafed with the clamours of their own dear groans, / Will hear your idle scorns, continue then, / And I will have you and that fault withal; / But if they will not, throw away that spirit, / And I shall find you empty of that fault, / Right joyful of your reformation.

Why, that's the way to choke a mocking spirit, whose power comes from the easy favour that shallow, laughing listeners give to fools. A joke's success lies in the ear of the person who hears it, never in the tongue of the person who makes it. So if sick ears, deafened by the noise of their own groans, will listen to your idle mockery, carry on, and I'll take you, fault and all; but if they won't, throw away that spirit, and I'll find you emptied of that fault and be very glad you've reformed.
A twelvemonth? Well, befall what will befall, / I'll jest a twelvemonth in an hospital.
A year? Well, come what may, I'll joke for a year in a hospital.
[To the King] Ay, sweet my lord, and so I take my leave.
[To the King] Yes, my sweet lord, and so I take my leave.
No, madam, we will bring you on your way.
No, madam, we'll escort you on your way.
Our wooing doth not end like an old play. / Jack hath not Jill. These ladies' courtesy / Might well have made our sport a comedy.
Our wooing doesn't end like an old play: Jack doesn't get his Jill. These ladies, if they'd been kind, could easily have made our sport a comedy.
Come, sir, it wants a twelvemonth and a day, / And then 'twill end.
Come, sir, it's only a year and a day away, and then it'll end that way.
That's too long for a play.
That's too long for a play.

I will kiss thy royal finger, and take leave. I am a votary; I have / vowed to Jaquenetta to hold the plough for her sweet love three year. / But, most esteemed Greatness, will you hear the dialogue that the two / learned men have compiled in praise of the owl and the cuckoo? It / should have followed in the end of our show.

I will kiss your royal finger and take my leave. I am under a vow: I have sworn to Jaquenetta to work the plough for her sweet love for three years. But, most esteemed Greatness, will you hear the dialogue the two learned men have written in praise of the owl and the cuckoo? It should have come at the end of our show.
Call them forth quickly; we will do so.
Call them out quickly; we will.
This side is Hiems, Winter; this Ver, the Spring; the one / maintained by the owl, th' other by the cuckoo. Ver, begin.
This side is Hiems, Winter; this is Ver, Spring; one is represented by the owl, the other by the cuckoo. Ver, begin.

When daisies pied and violets blue / And lady-smocks all silver-white / And cuckoo-buds of yellow hue / Do paint the meadows with delight, / The cuckoo then on every tree / Mocks married men; for thus sings he: / "Cuckoo! / Cuckoo, cuckoo!" O, word of fear, / Unpleasing to a married ear. / When shepherds pipe on oaten straws, / And merry larks are ploughmen's clocks, / When turtles tread, and rooks and daws, / And maidens bleach their summer smocks, / The cuckoo then, on every tree, / Mocks married men, for thus sings he: / "Cuckoo! / Cuckoo, cuckoo!" O, word of fear, / Unpleasing to a married ear.

(Song) When speckled daisies and blue violets, silver-white lady's-smocks and yellow buttercups paint the meadows with delight, then the cuckoo in every tree mocks married men, because this is what it sings: 'Cuckoo! Cuckoo, cuckoo!' Oh, word of fear (cuckold!), unpleasant to a married man's ear. When shepherds play pipes of oat straw, and merry larks wake the ploughmen like clocks, when turtle-doves, rooks and jackdaws mate, and girls bleach their summer smocks in the sun, then the cuckoo in every tree mocks married men, because this is what it sings: 'Cuckoo! Cuckoo, cuckoo!' Oh, word of fear, unpleasant to a married man's ear.

When icicles hang by the wall, / And Dick the shepherd blows his nail, / And Tom bears logs into the hall, / And milk comes frozen home in pail, / When blood is nipped, and ways be foul, / Then nightly sings the staring owl: / "Tu-whit, Tu-whoo!" A merry note, / While greasy Joan doth keel the pot. / When all aloud the wind doth blow, / And coughing drowns the parson's saw, / And birds sit brooding in the snow, / And Marian's nose looks red and raw, / When roasted crabs hiss in the bowl, / Then nightly sings the staring owl: / "Tu-whit, Tu-whoo!" A merry note, / While greasy Joan doth keel the pot.

(Song) When icicles hang by the wall, and Dick the shepherd blows on his fingernails, and Tom carries logs into the hall, and the milk comes home frozen in the pail, when blood is chilled and roads are muddy, then every night the staring owl sings 'Tu-whit, tu-whoo!', a merry note, while greasy Joan stirs the pot to stop it boiling over. When the wind blows loudly, and coughing drowns out the parson's sermon, and birds sit brooding in the snow, and Marian's nose looks red and raw, when roasted crab-apples hiss in the bowl of punch, then every night the staring owl sings 'Tu-whit, tu-whoo!', a merry note, while greasy Joan stirs the pot.
The words of Mercury are harsh after the songs of Apollo. / You that way, we this way.
The words of Mercury, the messenger, are harsh after the songs of Apollo. You go that way; we'll go this way.
